Dysregulation of sirtuin activity, particularly sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) and sirtuin 3 (SIRT3), has been implicated in the pathogenesis of cardiometabolic diseases, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Under conditions of nutrient excess, alterations in acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) and NAD+ availability promote mitochondrial protein hyperacetylation, contributing to impaired mitochondrial respiration. Evidence from genetic and proteomic studies across metabolically active tissues such as the liver, heart, adipose tissue, skeletal muscle and pancreatic β-cells, highlight a central role for sirtuins in maintaining metabolic homeostasis. Therapeutic strategies aimed at improving mitochondrial function through activation of sirtuins have gained significant attention. Early studies focused on natural sirtuin activators, such as resveratrol and honokiol, while subsequent efforts led to the development of synthetic small-molecule activators, although their mechanisms of action remain debated. More recently, small molecule activators of SIRT1, such as SRT2104, and SIRT3, such as 2-acetyl-4-phenylquinoline (2-AQPC) and SZC-6 have been identified. In parallel, NAD+ augmenting through supplementation of NAD+ precursors such as nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide mononucleotide has shown similar promising metabolic benefits in preclinical rodent models. Sirtuin-mediated lysine deacetylation represents a central mechanism regulating metabolic function and a promising target for therapeutic intervention in cardiometabolic disease.

articles.title: Possibilities for Cytoprotective Liver Therapy, Stable Gastric Pentadecapeptide BPC 157, and Standard Agents-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Cytoprotection provides a conceptual framework for the preservation and restoration of tissue integrity under conditions of noxious injury. In liver disease, however, effective protection may require more than direct limitation of hepatocellular damage, encompassing endothelial function, microcirculation, vascular homeostasis, oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, and portal hemodynamics. This review examines possibilities for cytoprotective liver therapy, with particular emphasis on stable gastric pentadecapeptide BPC 157 and comparison with established or experimentally investigated agents, including N-acetylcysteine, ursodeoxycholic acid, corticosteroids, resveratrol, L-arginine, curcumin, sildenafil, VEGF-related approaches, stem cell therapies, melatonin, simvastatin, prostacyclin analogues, and coenzyme Q10. Evidence is considered across representative experimental models of acetaminophen and carbon tetrachloride hepatotoxicity, bile duct ligation, and alcohol-induced liver injury. The diversity of effective agents indicates that liver injury involves multiple interconnected pathological mechanisms and that preservation of hepatocellular integrity may be achieved through different pharmacological pathways. BPC 157 is distinguished by evidence of beneficial effects across these major models and additional vascular and occlusion/occlusion-like syndromes. In particular, reported findings indicate prevention and reversal of experimentally induced portal hypertension, including prehepatic, intrahepatic, and posthepatic disturbances, together with attenuation of hepatic congestion, thrombosis, oxidative injury, and associated multiorgan dysfunction. These findings support the concept that cytoprotection may extend from hepatoprotection to restoration of vascular and tissue homeostasis. Collectively, the available preclinical evidence supports further investigation of integrated cytoprotective strategies for liver injury. Nevertheless, experimental evidence, however extensive, does not establish clinical efficacy, and appropriately designed clinical studies remain necessary to determine therapeutic applicability in human liver disease.

articles.title: Traditional Mexican Medicinal Plants for Ocular Diseases: Ethnomedicinal Evidence, Pharmacological Relevance, and Research Gaps from Unexplored Sources.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Traditional medicinal knowledge remains underrepresented in pharmacological research because much of it is preserved in printed monographs, institutional collections, historical documents, and non-digitized ethnomedical repositories. This study aimed to document medicinal plants used in Mexican traditional medicine for ocular disorders and identify taxa of ethnomedicinal and pharmacological relevance. Methods: Three repositories were examined: the Medicinal Herbarium of the Mexican Institute of Social Security (IMSS), the open-access Biblioteca de la Medicina Tradicional Mexicana, and a pioneering undergraduate thesis addressing Mexican medicinal plants used for ophthalmological conditions. Data were manually extracted by two independent expert reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Botanical nomenclature was updated using World Flora Online, and records were compared with previous Mexican ethnomedicinal information. Available pharmacological evidence was considered to contextualize the ethnomedical findings and identify taxa warranting further investigation. Results: The present contribution documented 232 ethnomedicinal records, corresponding to 174 species, 124 genera, and 57 botanical families. Asteraceae represented the predominant family, while Matricaria chamomilla was identified as the most frequently cited species. Notably, 165 ethnomedicinal records corresponding to 142 species identified in this work were absent from previous analysis of Mexican medicinal plants for ocular diseases, demonstrating the value of these repositories. Species such as Argemone ochroleuca exhibited notable ethnomedical relevance despite the limited pharmacological and clinical evidence currently available. Conclusions: The present work expands the existing ethnopharmacological knowledge of Mexican medicinal plants used for ocular diseases and highlights the value of integrating historical, institutional and digital sources into modern ethnopharmacological research. Furthermore, the findings identify and prioritize selected taxa for further pharmacological, toxicological, and formulations studies with potential ophthalmological applications.

articles.title: Historical Perspective and Clinical Implementation of Pharmacogenomics (PGx) Technology with Clinical Decision Support (CDS) in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry.
articles.abstract: Pharmacogenomics (PGx) uses the variation in a patient's genetic profile to assist with medication choice, with the goal of shortening the trial-and-error process of prescribing in psychiatry. Over the past few decades, PGx technology has evolved greatly to identify various genetic polymorphisms in drug-metabolizing enzymes; however, clinical use and relevance of PGx in child and adolescent psychiatry (CAAP) remain limited. This narrative review explores the historical evolution of PGx, compares key technological advancements, and evaluates their clinical relevance to CAAP. We address current barriers to PGx implementation, including developmental differences in pharmacokinetics between adults and children, the lack of robust evidence of clinical efficacy in youth populations, and inconsistent guidelines causing clinician confusion. We also highlight the need for clinical decision support (CDS) tools and broader practical and ethical considerations before widespread uptake of PGx would be feasible.

articles.title: Opioid Peptide Hybrids as Multifunctional Analgesic Ligands: Emphasis on Intracellular Signaling.
articles.abstract: Opioid peptide hybrids are multifunctional molecules in which an opioid pharmacophore is covalently integrated with a second opioid or non-opioid pharmacophore within a single molecular entity. Their development is driven by a major challenge in analgesic pharmacotherapy: although μ-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists remain among the most effective agents for the treatment of moderate-to-severe pain, their therapeutic use is limited by adverse effects and risks associated particularly with prolonged or high-dose exposure, including tolerance, constipation, respiratory depression, physical dependence, and abuse liability. Especially, chronic and neuropathic pain involves complex interactions among multiple receptor systems, neurotransmitter networks, and intracellular signaling pathways. Accordingly, hybrid peptide ligands provide a rational multitarget strategy aimed at achieving analgesia through the coordinated modulation of complementary pharmacological targets rather than selective modulation of a single receptor system. This approach may enhance analgesic efficacy and potentially improve the therapeutic profile of opioid-based treatments by reducing some of the dose-limiting adverse effects associated with conventional opioid analgesics. In this review, we discuss the functional and pharmacological interactions between opioid receptors and other receptor systems involved in pain perception and modulation, with emphasis on those for which peptide-based hybrid ligands with demonstrated antinociceptive activity have been developed.

articles.title: Plant-Derived Control of Postprandial Glycemia: α-Amylase, α-Glucosidase, and the Incretin-DPP-4 Interface.
articles.abstract: Postprandial hyperglycemia can be modified before absorbed glucose reaches the circulation. Plant-derived compounds may slow starch hydrolysis through α-amylase and intestinal α-glucosidases, stimulate glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) release, or preserve incretin activity through dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibition. This critical narrative review integrates these mechanisms around intestinal exposure, substrate selectivity, and human evidence. Flavonoids show structure-dependent and time-dependent inhibition of carbohydrate-hydrolyzing enzymes, but results vary markedly between yeast, rodent, and human enzyme systems. Iminosugar-rich mulberry preparations and thiosugar-containing Salacia extracts provide the strongest chemistry-to-clinic examples, including randomized trials that reduced postprandial glucose or HbA1c. Preclinical studies suggest that berberine may link bitter-taste-receptor-mediated GLP-1 secretion with local intestinal DPP-4 effects, whereas mangiferin, flavonol glycosides, anthocyanins, and food-derived peptides remain supported mainly by preclinical studies. In vitro potency alone is insufficient: meal composition, enzyme source, luminal concentration, metabolism, product standardization, gastrointestinal tolerance, and incretin measurements determine translational value. Candidate prioritization requires defined chemistry, achievable exposure, and product-specific human validation; acute effects do not establish durable benefit or human target engagement.

articles.title: Mechanisms, Discovery Strategies, and Emerging Opportunities for AI-Assisted Design of Peptides in Cosmetics and Skin Health.
articles.abstract: Synthetic peptides are increasingly used in cosmetic products due to their potential to regulate biological processes related to skin aging, pigmentation, inflammation, extracellular matrix maintenance, and other aspects of skin health. However, the mechanisms of many cosmetic peptides are still not fully understood. Their activities can also be limited by poor stability, skin penetration, off-target effects, and limited clinical evidence. This review discusses the major classes of cosmetic peptides and the molecular mechanisms through which they are proposed to exert their activities. It also examines the main approaches used for peptide discovery. These include discovery from natural and biologically derived sources, library-based screening, rational design, and classical computational methods. More recent artificial intelligence (AI)-guided approaches are then discussed, with particular attention to structure-based and sequence-based peptide design. AI provides new opportunities to search much larger peptide sequence spaces and to prioritize candidates before experimental testing. Structure-based methods can use information about target binding sites to guide peptide design, while sequence-based approaches can identify interaction patterns without requiring detailed 3D structural information. These methods may also help improve peptide specificity, reduce potential off-target interactions, and identify naturally occurring peptides with useful properties. Although the application of AI to cosmetic peptide discovery is still at an early stage, it may provide a useful addition to existing approaches. Future progress will depend on better skin-relevant datasets, improved experimental validation, and design strategies that consider not only target binding, but also selectivity, stability, toxicity, delivery, and formulation compatibility.

articles.title: Polysaccharide-Derived Drug Delivery Systems: Therapeutic Potential in Rheumatoid Arthritis-A Review.
articles.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by chronic synovial inflammation, synovial hyperplasia, and progressive joint destruction and remains a major clinical challenge. Polysaccharide-derived delivery platforms have attracted widespread attention for RA precision therapy owing to their natural origin, excellent biocompatibility, and tailorable functionality; however, existing reviews generally focus on single material or carrier types and provide limited cross-comparison of carrier architectures and translational considerations. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in polysaccharide derivative design strategies and delivery system innovations for RA management. We first elaborate on how chemical modifications confer multi-responsive properties (pH-, reactive oxygen species [ROS]-, and enzyme-triggered release) and how diversified morphologies (hydrogels, microspheres, microneedles, vesicles) enable spatiotemporally controlled drug delivery in inflamed joints. Critical analysis highlights several translational barriers, including limited in vivo retention, insufficient pharmacokinetic and biodistribution data, and challenges associated with scale-up manufacturing and reproducibility. Looking forward, future development should integrate biomimetic design, rational multi-component optimization, and advanced manufacturing technologies to improve the stability, controllability, and translational feasibility of polysaccharide-based RA delivery systems. This review provides an integrated, translation-focused perspective that bridges material engineering and clinical pathological demands, guiding the development of next-generation polysaccharide-based RA therapies.

articles.title: Nanoparticle-Mediated and Nanoengineered Drug Delivery for Glaucoma: Preclinical Evidence, Early Human Feasibility, and Translational Challenges.
articles.abstract: The management of glaucoma with drugs is mostly via the topical route, although these treatments have poor ocular bioavailability. Other problems limiting their therapeutic effect include pre-corneal clearance, corneal and ocular surface barriers, and the need for a long-term treatment regimen. Nanoparticle-mediated drug-delivery systems have shown the potential, particularly in preclinical studies, to improve ocular penetration and precorneal retention and to facilitate controlled drug release, with the aim of reducing dosing frequency. In this narrative review, the researchers focus on various nanoparticle-based approaches for sustained intraocular pressure control in glaucoma. The review encompasses carrier-based nanosystems, drug nanocrystals and nanosuspensions, nanoscale permeability or surface modifiers, multiscale nano-enabled formulations, and nanoparticle- or nanocarrier-integrated delivery devices. These approaches are designed to deliver conventional and innovative ocular hypotensive agents. Pharmacokinetics, corneal permeability, drug stability, tolerability, and duration of action of intraocular pressure-lowering drugs are critically reviewed across a predominantly preclinical evidence base; the two small human studies identified (n = 6 and n = 17) support clinical feasibility but do not establish durable clinical effectiveness, long-term safety, adherence benefit, or prevention of glaucoma progression. This review distinguishes improvements in ocular drug disposition from demonstrated IOP-lowering benefit and separates preclinical proof of concept from human evidence by applying an evidence-stratified formulation-performance framework rather than ranking nanocarriers by material class or isolated physicochemical properties. The available evidence is dominated by drugs that lower IOP, which in turn distinguishes prolonged control of IOP from any direct disease-modifying or neuroprotective action, for which glaucoma-specific evidence remains substantially more limited. The review further assesses the obstacles to clinical translation, including long-term safety, manufacturing reproducibility, sterilization, regulatory requirements, and patient and treatment burden. Generally, nanoengineered systems are promising platforms to address pharmacokinetic and treatment-delivery limitations of conventional glaucoma therapy, but comparative clinical effectiveness, long-term safety, adherence benefit, cost-effectiveness, and meaningful effects on glaucoma progression remain insufficiently demonstrated.

articles.title: Unlocking the Full Potential of Taylor Dispersion Analysis Through Advanced Detection.
articles.abstract: Today, pharmaceutical sciences rely on a wide range of innovative therapeutics of varying sizes: nanoparticles, proteins, antibodies, and nanocarriers for drug delivery. Measuring their size is one of the crucial parameters in their characterization, to ensure drug safety, stability, and effectiveness. Over the past two decades, Taylor Dispersion Analysis has emerged as an important sizing method. Its scope of application is perfectly suited to the sizes of these therapeutics. By design, it can be coupled with a wide range of detectors, and extensive research has been conducted in this field. In this review, we will present an overview of the studies conducted, and discuss how the application drives the choice of one detector or another (size measurement, aggregation studies, interaction studies, and other analyses, performed in both simple biological buffers and in more complex media, particularly serum) and makes Taylor Dispersion Analysis a highly versatile tool.

articles.title: Pathophysiology and Comprehensive Pharmacological Management of ATTR Cardiac Amyloidosis: Knowledge Gaps, Ongoing Clinical Trials, and Future Research Directions.
articles.abstract: The purpose of this review article is to discuss the current treatment modalities and ongoing clinical trials regarding cardiac amyloidosis (CA), specifically transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA). Amyloidosis refers to the extracellular deposition of insoluble amyloid fibrillar proteins. When these proteins are deposited in the heart's myocardium, it is referred to as cardiac amyloidosis. CA can be divided into two main groups: light chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL-CA) and transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA), which can be further subdivided into wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRwt) and hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv). ATTR-CA is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure in the setting of progressive restrictive cardiomyopathy, particularly among older adults, males, and individuals of African descent, with remarkable advances in the therapeutic landscape. TTR stabilizers, including Tafamidis (approved in 2019) and Acoramidis (approved in 2024), have demonstrated significant reductions in mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations. Gene silencing therapies, including Vutrisiran (approved in 2025), represent a new drug group that targets TTR production at the RNA level. Meanwhile, CRISPR-based gene editing with nexiguran ziclumeran (nex-z or NTLA-2001) and amyloid-depleting monoclonal antibodies offer the prospect of one-time curative treatments and active fibril clearance, respectively. However, despite these advances, substantial knowledge gaps persist: no head-to-head trials have compared stabilizers to silencers, optimal combination therapy regimens remain undefined, and the role of conventional guideline-directed medical therapy in ATTR-CA has only been supported by observational data.

articles.title: When Does Magnesium Stearate Improve Carrier-Based Dry Powder Inhalers (DPI) Performance? A Critical Review of Material, Process, and Formulation Factors.
articles.abstract: Magnesium stearate (MgSt), although well established as a pharmaceutical lubricant in solid oral dosage forms, plays a more complex role in carrier-based dry powder inhalers (DPIs), where it functions as a surface modifier and force control agent (FCA). In DPI formulations, MgSt can influence powder rheology, moisture resistance, interparticulate interactions, and aerosolization efficiency; however, these effects depend not simply on its presence or concentration, but on whether effective surface modification is achieved. This review critically evaluates experimental evidence on MgSt-mediated particle coating in carrier-based DPIs, with particular emphasis on how material attributes, particle cohesion and surface area, process energy, coating strategy, and MgSt concentration interact to determine coating efficiency and formulation performance. By integrating these factors, the review aims to provide a mechanistic framework for selecting and optimizing MgSt coating strategies and to identify methodological priorities for future research. The available evidence indicates that process energy is a major determinant of coating efficiency. High-energy techniques, particularly mechanofusion, can effectively modify highly cohesive micronized particles that are difficult to coat using conventional blending, whereas high-shear blending may provide sufficient energy for surface modification of larger, coarse lactose carriers. Mechanical milling represents a distinct strategy in which particle-size reduction and surface modification occur simultaneously. Direct comparison between coating approaches remains difficult because studies differ in MgSt grade, carrier and API properties, particle size distribution, processing conditions, and methods used to assess coating efficiency. MgSt generally improves aerosolization by modifying cohesive and adhesive interactions, but the magnitude of this effect is formulation-specific. Improvements in fine-particle delivery depend on MgSt particle size and specific surface area, the properties and surface area of the particles being coated, process energy, and the resulting coating efficiency. Consequently, increasing MgSt concentration does not necessarily improve performance, and excessive amounts may lead to overlubrication or MgSt agglomeration. Despite considerable progress, important knowledge gaps remain regarding how MgSt coating translates into improved DPI performance. Further studies integrating material properties, processing conditions, surface modification, and formulation performance are needed to establish more robust relationships between coating strategy and functional outcomes. Such knowledge may support more rational and formulation-specific use of MgSt in carrier-based DPIs.

articles.title: Treasures from the Ocean: Deciphering the Therapeutic Utility of Marine-Derived ACE-Inhibitory Peptides in Cardiovascular Drug Discovery.
articles.abstract: Marine-derived bioactive peptides show significant promise as candidates for cardiovascular drug discovery because of their diverse biological activities and ACE-inhibitory activity. This review outlines the current state of knowledge on marine-derived ACE-inhibitory peptides as potential therapeutic targets for cardiovascular drug discovery. This narrative review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases with a focus on eligible studies on ACE inhibition; peptide sequence and structural characteristics; hydrolysis and purification approaches; molecular docking; pharmacokinetic strategies; drug discovery; drug-delivery approaches; and clinical studies. This review shows that ACE-inhibitory peptides are derived from marine organisms. The reviewed studies report peptide activity determined by amino acid composition, peptide length, hydrophobicity, hydrolysis method, fractionation, chromatographic purification, and characterization techniques. Computer-based molecular mechanism studies further demonstrate that marine peptides interact with ACE through hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and interactions at the catalytic subsite surrounding the Zn ion center. Most of the peptides have demonstrated antihypertensive effects in animal models, while limited clinical evidence suggests potential for further development. This review concludes that marine-derived ACE-inhibitory peptides are promising targets for cardiovascular drug discovery. Clinical translational barriers, industrial-scale production, clinical validation, and regulatory approval are essential to address in future work. Integration of molecular docking, advanced delivery approaches, medicinal chemistry, AI-assisted peptide design, sustainable green extraction, and clinical research could expedite their translation into pharmaceutical approaches for further drug development.

articles.title: Endophyte-Mediated Green Synthesis of Metallic Nanoparticles: Mechanistic Insights, Antibiofilm Efficacy, and Translational Challenges.
articles.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance, a major health problem for the world's population, is caused by pathogenic bacteria capable of forming biofilms, claiming 4.95 million lives each year, according to WHO (World Health Organization) data, and could escalate up to 10 million annual deaths by 2050 if unchecked. Biofilms are the structured microbial populations surrounded and composed by an EPS (Extracellular Polymeric Substance) matrix to protect themselves from host immune responses and antibiotics, which makes the infections persistent and difficult to treat. Current global approaches to the pathogenic microbes to address AMR (Antimicrobial Resistance) are solved by different alternative strategies; one such strategy is nanotechnology, a rapidly developing field in the twenty-first century, using metallic nanoparticles that are generally characterized by dimensions within the range of 1-100 nm, have distinct structural and functional properties from bulk materials, and perform higher penetration in the cell membranes of pathogenic microbes. Overall, the present review offers a detailed overview of significant knowledge gaps regarding scalability, long-term safety, and the mechanistic pathway of nanoparticles synthesized from endophytic microorganisms. The inclusion also summarizes a comparison of bacterial and fungal endophyte-mediated metallic nanoparticles with plant-mediated metallic nanoparticles, particularly in terms of metabolite diversity, synthesis efficiency, size, nanoparticle stability, toxicity, antimicrobial activity, and antibiofilm potential. The novelty lies in how the efficacy of endophytic-mediated metallic nanoparticles acts against the defense mechanisms of pathogenic microorganisms in terms of molecular pathways and processes associated with ROS (Reactive Oxygen Species), disruption of membrane integrity, quorum sensing interference, EPS (Extracellular Polymeric Substance) degradation, DNA and protein disruption, and biofilm collapse. However, nanoparticles synthesized from endophytic microorganisms face translational challenges and limitations that need to be addressed.

articles.title: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia Beyond BCR::ABL1 Inhibition: Resistance Mechanisms and Emerging Therapeutic Modalities.
articles.abstract: The BCR::ABL1 fusion oncoprotein is the molecular hallmark and principal oncogenic driver of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have transformed CML into a largely manageable chronic disease, yet acquired resistance, persistence of leukemic stem cells (LSCs), and disease progression remain important therapeutic challenges. This narrative review examines the molecular and cellular determinants of TKI resistance and their implications for current and emerging therapeutic strategies. Resistance involves both BCR::ABL1-dependent and -independent mechanisms, ranging from kinase-domain mutations to adaptive signaling, altered drug transport, microenvironmental protection, metabolic reprogramming, and epigenetic dysregulation. Increasing understanding of these processes has yielded therapeutic strategies with growing clinical relevance, including next-generation TKIs, dual-site BCR::ABL1 inhibition, as well as rational combination approaches targeting alternative signaling and other survival dependencies. At the experimental frontier, PROTAC-mediated protein degradation, siRNA-based gene silencing, and CAR-based cellular immunotherapies are being explored as innovative approaches for targeting resistant leukemic populations. Nanotechnology-based delivery systems further provide opportunities for targeted delivery of TKIs and nucleic-acid therapeutics. In parallel, molecular monitoring and multi-omic profiling offer opportunities to better define disease evolution and guide individualized treatment. The continued translation of these advances into clinically applicable therapeutic strategies may help address the unmet therapeutic needs in CML, especially in the setting of advanced and blast-phase disease.

articles.title: Clinically Anchored GPCR Drug Discovery: Translational Lessons from Success, Failure, and Post-Approval Reassessment.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: G protein-coupled receptors are a productive drug target family, yet clinical performance varies widely across rare, immune-mediated, pain, and thromboinflammatory diseases. We aimed to construct an explicit, stage-gated framework that makes translational prioritisation auditable and to examine whether it distinguishes clinically successful from unsuccessful programmes. Methods: This narrative, clinically anchored review included programmes with a stated human-disease rationale, Phase 2 or later clinical experience or a regulatory decision, and publicly accessible primary or regulatory documentation; evidence was considered through 7 August 2026. The cases spanned rare disease, immune-mediated inflammation, pain, and thromboinflammation. Thirteen programmes were reviewed, and eleven were entered into a retrospective five-axis scorecard covering human-disease anchoring, receptor pharmacology, modality and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic feasibility, biomarker-to-endpoint readiness, and durability. Each axis was scored 0-2, weighted to 100 points, and subject to predefined hard-stop rules. Results: Established successes scored 80-100 points, whereas failed programmes scored 30-48. PAR4 scored 57.5 and therefore fell in the stop-and-rework band; avacopan scored 80 before approval but now triggers an Axis 5 hard stop. Equal weighting preserved the classifications of established successes and hard-stop failures but shifted PAR4 to 60.0, demonstrating sensitivity of a borderline programme to the weighting scheme. The scorecard localized failures mainly to redundancy, biomarker-endpoint disconnect, or durability/evidence-integrity gates. Conclusions: The framework is an explicit prioritisation aid, not an externally validated predictive model. Its main value is to identify missing evidence and non-compensable weaknesses; prospective independent validation, including inter-rater reliability testing, is required before portfolio use.

articles.title: Natural Modulators of the PPARγ-Adiponectin Axis in Insulin Resistance: Structural Pharmacology, Receptor-State Selectivity, and Translational Readiness.
articles.abstract: Insulin resistance reflects maladaptive communication among adipose tissue, the liver, skeletal muscle, immune cells, and the vasculature. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is a validated insulin-sensitizing target, but classical full agonism couples metabolic efficacy to weight gain, fluid retention, and skeletal liability. This critical narrative review evaluates plant-derived and dietary molecules through a receptor-state framework that distinguishes direct binding from reporter activation and separates full agonism, partial agonism, selective modulation, antagonism with retained metabolic function, and post-translational control of PPARγ. Adiponectin is considered a functional inter-organ circuit linking adipocyte PPARγ activity to AdipoR1/AdipoR2 signaling, AMPK, PPARα, ceramide metabolism, glucose disposal, and fatty-acid oxidation. Amorfrutins provide the most coherent target-led natural-product evidence, whereas chelerythrine offers a structurally defined selective-modulation benchmark; honokiol, diosmin, betulinic acid, valerenic acid, punicic acid, alkamides, and defined extracts show heterogeneous mechanistic and translational maturity. Human evidence linking natural PPARγ ligands to verified target engagement and improved insulin sensitivity remains limited. We therefore propose a seven-stage translational roadmap connecting chemical identity, orthogonal binding, receptor-state pharmacology, cellular function, tissue exposure, mechanism-matched safety, and randomized human proof.

articles.title: Beyond Weight Loss and Glycemic Control: Molecular Mechanisms and Hypothesis-Generating Therapeutic Potential of Incretin-Based Therapies Against Peritoneal Fibrosis in Peritoneal Dialysis.
articles.abstract: Background: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is an established kidney replacement therapy, but long-term exposure to bioincompatible dialysate, uremic toxins, recurrent peritonitis, glucose degradation products, oxidative stress, and sterile inflammation progressively remodels the peritoneal membrane and contributes to peritoneal fibrosis (PF). This review summarizes the molecular basis of PF in PD and evaluates the therapeutic rationale for incretin-based interventions beyond weight loss and glycemic control. Methods: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, translational, and clinically relevant literature on PD-associated PF, with emphasis on DPP-4 biology, GLP-1 receptor agonism, inflammatory and oxidative signaling, angiogenesis, mesothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, glycemic management in PD, and selected author-conducted translational studies interpreted alongside independent evidence. Results: Available evidence supports a model in which DPP-4 activation, altered GLP-1/GLP-1R signaling, TGF-β/Smad3-driven mesothelial transition, NF-κB/MyD88 inflammation, ROS-mediated oxidative stress, angiogenesis, apoptosis, and cytoskeletal remodeling converge to impair peritoneal membrane integrity. DPP-4 inhibition, exendin-4, and dulaglutide attenuated these pathways in experimental models, while GLP-1 receptor agonists have established metabolic benefits in appropriate diabetic and obese populations. Conclusions: Direct clinical evidence that incretin-based therapies prevent or treat peritoneal fibrosis in humans undergoing PD is currently lacking. Therefore, peritoneal membrane protection, reduced ultrafiltration failure, and improved technique survival should be regarded as investigational, hypothesis-generating possibilities that require prospective clinical validation.

articles.title: Cell Type- and Phase-Dependent Immune Checkpoint Targeting in Sepsis: TIM-3 as a Model for Precision Immunomodulation.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a dysregulated host response in which hyperinflammation, immunoparalysis, lymphoid depletion, myeloid dysfunction, tissue injury and defective pathogen control frequently coexist and evolve over time. Immune checkpoint pathways have therefore attracted interest as candidates for immune restoration, but receptor upregulation alone is an unreliable therapeutic signal. This review develops a cell type- and phase-dependent framework for immune checkpoint targeting in sepsis, using TIM-3 as a model checkpoint node. We first discuss the conceptual pitfalls in translating checkpoint blockade from cancer and chronic infection to acute heterogeneous sepsis. We then examine why the immune phase should be defined by dynamic host response states rather than by the clock time and why checkpoint signals must be interpreted according to their cellular source, including effector lymphocytes, NKT cells, CD4+ T cells, monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells and suppressive myeloid populations. TIM-3 illustrates this complexity. In sepsis-relevant studies, TIM-3 has been linked to NKT cell and hepatic CD8+ T-cell apoptosis, CD4/HMGB1/TIM-3-associated hyporesponsiveness, Galectin-9-related ligand effects and potential myeloid or tissue-resident functions involving phosphatidylserine-positive debris, extracellular vesicles and tissue homeostasis. These observations argue against treating TIM-3 as a single-purpose inhibitory receptor or assuming that antibody blockade, ligand administration, receptor mutation and Galectin-glycan interference perturb the same biology. We propose that future checkpoint-directed studies should enroll immune states rather than syndromic sepsis alone; integrate the inflammatory burden, innate immune competence, lymphoid function and ligand context; and prioritize mechanistic endpoints such as lymphocyte apoptosis, IFN-γ recovery, monocyte HLA-DR restoration, LPS-induced TNF responses, bacterial clearance and secondary infection. Future precision immunomodulation studies in sepsis should evaluate defined checkpoint-associated circuits rather than infer therapeutic relevance from receptor expression alone.

articles.title: Population Pharmacokinetic Models of Voriconazole in Pediatric Patients: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Voriconazole dosing in children is complicated by developmental and nonlinear pharmacokinetics, cytochrome P450 2C19 (CYP2C19) variation, variable oral bioavailability, inflammation, organ dysfunction, and drug interactions. We evaluated the characteristics, reporting completeness, and clinical applicability of pediatric and pediatric-inclusive voriconazole population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models. Methods: PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and supplementary sources were searched from inception to 12 March 2026. Eligible studies developed a voriconazole PopPK model in patients aged 0-18 years or in a broader population with extractable or interpretable pediatric information. Reporting completeness was assessed using the 32-item Clinical Pharmacokinetic (ClinPK) checklist. Results: Eighteen studies published from 2004 to 2025 were included. Model-development cohorts contained 21-173 participants, and 15 studies reported 108-3336 concentrations. The median ClinPK reporting-completeness score was 82.6% (range, 74.2-90.0%). The included studies comprised one infant-specific, nine pediatric-only, six pediatric-young adult, and two mixed pediatric-adult models. Fifteen studies used parametric nonlinear mixed-effects methods and three used nonparametric methods; 15 selected two-compartment models and three selected one-compartment models. Body size was incorporated in 17 models and CYP2C19 phenotype was the most frequent retained covariate (10 models). Elimination structures, exposure targets, and dosing proposals were heterogeneous, and only one model underwent independent external validation. Conclusions: A population-matched model may support initial dosing, but early therapeutic drug monitoring and iterative Bayesian updating remain necessary. Current evidence does not support a universal pediatric model. Independent external validation and prospective implementation studies are required before routine clinical use.

articles.title: Advanced Nucleic Acid Architectures: Classification, Assembly Mechanisms, and Biomedical Applications.
articles.abstract: Nucleic acids are increasingly exploited as programmable molecular materials for nanomedicine, biosensing, and biomaterials engineering, but their biomedical deployment remains constrained by nuclease degradation, inefficient membrane transport, endosomal sequestration, rapid clearance, and potential immune activation. This Review presents a role-based framework for advanced nucleic acid architectures according to the contribution of nucleic acids to final structure, spanning nucleic acid-dictated architectures, supramolecular nucleic acid co-assemblies, and nucleic acid-loaded composite biomaterials, including sequence-defined genetic cargos and non-sequence-defined PDRN-based regenerative systems. We compare sequence-directed hybridization, electrostatic condensation, metal-ligand coordination, polyamine- and polyphenol-mediated interactions, and carrier- or matrix-confined assembly, and relate these mechanisms to structural stability, nuclease resistance, cellular transport, intracellular release, stimulus responsiveness, and biological activity. Applications in drug and nucleic acid delivery, molecular diagnostics, regenerative and skin-repair biomaterials, vaccination, and immunomodulation are critically evaluated. Across platforms, architecture emerges as a formulation variable that must balance molecular protection with functional release, productive delivery, biosafety, and manufacturability. Translational development requires quantitative structure-performance relationships, standardized characterization, stability assessment, scalable processing, and context-specific pharmacokinetic and regulatory evaluation. This integrated perspective provides design principles for the rational pharmaceutical development of advanced nucleic acid systems.

articles.title: Pharmaceutical 3D Printing Beyond Printability: Polymer Functions, Structural Design, and Predictable Drug Release.
articles.abstract: Oral solid dosage forms, due to their mature manufacturing processes and stability, have become the cornerstone of clinical drug therapy. However, fixed dosages, uniform components, and large-scale production may not meet increasingly complex personalized requirements. The emergence of 3D-printed drugs provides a potential solution to this challenge. Drug 3D printing has progressed beyond feasibility verification and is moving toward functional dosage form design. Current research primarily focuses on printability; however, this review integrates printing technology, polymer functionality, structural design, release behavior, and translational requirements, summarizing mainstream printing technologies, including Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), Direct Ink Writing/Semi-Solid Extrusion (DIW/SSE), Powder Bed Printing (SLS/BJ), and Photopolymerization (SLA/DLP). Polymers are classified according to drug release control functions, illustrating how modulation of porosity, filling density, shell thickness, material partitioning, and spatial drug distribution enables 3D-printed dosage forms with diverse therapeutic functions. These functions include immediate and sustained release, gastric retention, intestinal targeting, and sequential release of multiple components. This review provides guidance for technical selection, structural design, and formulation development of 3D-printed drugs, while highlighting major translational barriers, including limited printable excipients, empirical formulation development, insufficient structure-based release prediction, quality control challenges, and weak clinical evidence. Future progress requires close integration of material, process, structure, and performance, enabling 3D-printed drugs to evolve from individual prototypes into scalable, quality-controllable, and clinically translatable drug delivery systems.

articles.title: Host Defense Peptides for Intracellular Bacterial Infections: Overcoming Translational Barriers Through Peptide Engineering and Nanotechnology-Based Drug Delivery Systems.
articles.abstract: Intracellular bacterial infections represent a major therapeutic challenge due to the ability of pathogens to persist within host cells, evade host immune surveillance and exhibit reduced susceptibility to conventional antibiotics. Consequently, these infections are often associated with severe clinical manifestations, antibiotic resistance, treatment failure, and increased mortality. Host-directed therapies have emerged as a promising approach by strengthening host defense mechanisms through the modulation of innate and adaptive immune responses, thereby enhancing the clearance of intracellular pathogens. Among these strategies, host defense peptides (HDPs) have gained considerable attention as they combine broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity with the ability to modulate host immune responses. HDPs also regulate the hyperinflammatory phase of infection, thereby limiting excessive tissue damage and infection-associated complications. Despite the promising preclinical efficacy against bacterial infections, the clinical translation of peptide-based therapeutics is hindered mainly by its inherent pharmacokinetic limitations, including poor stability, rapid proteolytic degradation, and limited bioavailability. However, recent advances in rational peptide engineering and nanotechnology-based delivery systems have shown considerable promise in overcoming these limitations. This review discusses the mechanisms employed by intracellular bacterial pathogens to colonize and survive within host cells. We highlight the immunomodulatory role of HDPs in controlling intracellular bacterial infections and critically examine the major barriers limiting their clinical translation. Finally, we summarize recent advances in peptide engineering and targeted delivery strategies that facilitate the development of HDP-based therapeutics for the effective treatment of intracellular bacterial infections.

articles.title: Toward Long-Acting Injectable Antidepressants: Drug-Delivery Strategies, Clinical Considerations, and Regulatory Barriers.
articles.abstract: Long-acting injectable (LAI) systems may offer an alternative approach to antidepressant treatment by reducing reliance on daily oral medication, supporting adherence, limiting pharmacokinetic fluctuations, and maintaining therapeutic drug exposure over extended periods. These potential advantages may be particularly relevant for patients with recurrent depression or difficulty sustaining regular oral treatment. However, converting conventional antidepressants into clinically useful LAIs remains challenging because many drugs require substantial maintenance doses, have formulation-limiting physicochemical properties, and may require dose adjustment or prompt discontinuation in response to adverse effects. This review evaluates the feasibility of established and emerging depot technologies, including polymeric microspheres, in situ-forming depots, lipid- and oil-based systems, hydrogels, and hybrid or stimulus-responsive platforms, for sustained antidepressant delivery. It compares these approaches according to drug-loading capacity, release mechanisms, achievable dosing interval, injection-volume constraints, manufacturing scalability, sterilization, product robustness, safety, local tissue tolerability, and regulatory maturity. Major translational barriers include the high total drug mass required for many antidepressants, acceptable injection-volume limits, solvent and excipient safety, injection-site reactions, limited reversibility after administration, pharmacokinetic drug-interaction risk, difficulty developing predictive in vitro-in vivo correlations and demanding regulatory expectations for complex injectable products. The review also considers opportunities for coordinated long-acting combination therapy, personalized patient selection, digital adherence monitoring, and emerging biomaterials. Overall, successful LAI antidepressant development will require careful matching of the drug molecules, delivery platform, pharmacokinetic target, and intended patient population. Early products are most likely to rely on established depot technologies and prior confirmation of oral efficacy and tolerability before long-term administration.

articles.title: Drug Dosing During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients: A Practical Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Drug dosing during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is difficult in critically ill patients because drug exposure is influenced by both the patient and the extracorporeal treatment. This narrative review provides a practical overview of drug dosing during CRRT, while intermittent hemodialysis and sustained low-efficiency dialysis are discussed only where they provide relevant contextual or comparative information. It summarizes the main drug-related, patient-related, and treatment-related factors that influence extracorporeal drug clearance and discusses their clinical implications for commonly used drug classes. Loading and maintenance doses should be considered separately: loading doses depend mainly on volume of distribution and the need for early therapeutic exposure, whereas maintenance dosing depends on total clearance, including residual renal, extracorporeal, and non-renal clearance. Therapeutic drug monitoring can help guide dose adjustment when validated targets are available, while model-informed precision dosing may provide additional support in selected patients. The review also proposes an eight-step practical framework based on residual kidney function, the actual delivered CRRT prescription, drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, therapeutic monitoring, and repeated reassessment. Future approaches may combine real-time CRRT data with pharmacokinetic models to support more individualized dosing.

articles.title: Retrotransposons: A New Frontier in In Vivo Genome Engineering.
articles.abstract: Genome engineering has transformed cell therapy, but clinical implementation remains largely confined to ex vivo workflows followed by adoptive cell transfer. These approaches require costly manufacturing, often rely on viral vectors, and carry risks associated with unwanted genomic alterations. Recent advances in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable genome-editing components to be delivered directly to specific cell populations in vivo, eliminating the need for ex vivo manufacturing. Several RNA-based genome-editing approaches have entered clinical trials. Nevertheless, current in vivo approaches remain largely limited to gene disruption or small sequence modifications. Conventional integration of large payloads generally requires DNA donors, which can be immunogenic, have limited nuclear access, and pose substantial LNP formulation challenges. When expression of therapeutic proteins such as chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) is required, LNP-based approaches predominantly deliver mRNA, leading to transient expression, whereas many applications require durable expression through stable genomic integration. Retrotransposons offer a solution because they have naturally evolved to reverse-transcribe RNA templates directly into chromosomal DNA. Engineered retrotransposon-derived platforms can integrate multi-kilobase payloads from RNA without an exogenous DNA donor. These platforms combine durable expression with RNA-only delivery, but clinical translation requires safe permanent integration, copy-number control, efficient delivery of all required components, and sufficient activity in disease-relevant primary cells. In this review, we describe the classes of non-LTR retrotransposons; examine the design principles underlying their adaptation as genome-editing tools; and compare emerging platforms derived from R2, LINE-1, Vingi, and RTE elements. These systems support integration strategies ranging from naturally evolved insertion profiles, such as site-specific insertion into ribosomal DNA (rDNA) or dispersed genome-wide integration, to fully programmable insertion. Several retrotransposon-based platforms have demonstrated multi-kilobase payload insertion, functional engineering of primary human T cells, and in vivo activity in mouse or non-human primate models, demonstrating their clinical promise. We also discuss key translational challenges. With continued optimization, retrotransposon-based platforms have the potential to bridge the gap between transient RNA delivery and durable gene writing, establishing a versatile foundation for the next generation of in vivo genetic medicines.

articles.title: The Application Potential and Future Challenges of Plant-Derived Exosome-like Nanoparticles in the Treatment of Liver Diseases.
articles.abstract: Liver disease is a serious global health challenge, with high morbidity and mortality that put significant socioeconomic stress on society. Despite therapeutic advances, current regimens have been limited by rapid drug resistance and insufficient targeting accuracy, and there is an urgent need for new methods. Plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (PELNs) are a promising natural nanotherapeutic platform due to their low immunogenicity, high biocompatibility, and prolonged stability in biological fluids. We review the biological sources, basic properties, and key preparative techniques for PELNs and characterize their mechanisms of action and therapeutic use in common liver diseases. We analyze their multiple-target hepatoprotective mechanisms including liver-specific targeting pathways and reducing critical inflammatory and antioxidant cascades. We summarize the therapeutic performance of different PELNs in major hepatic models including hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatic fibrosis, alcohol-related liver disease, and acute liver failure, highlighting key plant sources, primary biological effects, and precise molecular pathways. Moreover, one of the major methodological contributions of this work is the proposal of a new recommended extraction framework based on differential and density gradient centrifugation, optimized specifically for different plant tissue types (leaves, roots/stems, and fruits) to minimize technical heterogeneity. Finally, we discuss the major challenges that impede clinical translation of these nanovesicles, including incompletely elucidated mechanisms, imperfect manufacturing practices, and inadequate safety evaluation mechanisms, pointing to important, useful directions for future applications in hepatology.

articles.title: Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles as Biomimetic Drug Delivery Systems: Design, Therapeutic Applications, and Translational Challenges.
articles.abstract: Biomimetic cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (CM-NPs) have emerged as a promising class of nanocarriers that integrate the tunable physicochemical properties of engineered nanoparticles with selected biological features of naturally derived cell membranes. By retaining membrane-associated proteins, lipids, glycans, and receptors, CM-NPs have demonstrated the potential to modulate immune recognition, prolong systemic circulation, improve biocompatibility, and facilitate disease-specific targeting; however, these effects depend on the membrane source, nanoparticle composition, coating integrity, fabrication method, and biological context. This review critically examines major membrane-engineering strategies, including lipid insertion, covalent conjugation, metabolic glycoengineering, and genetic modification, together with fabrication methods such as extrusion, sonication, electroporation, in situ polymerization, and microfluidics. Particular emphasis is placed on nanoparticles coated with erythrocyte, platelet, stem cell, immune cell, bacterial, cancer cell, and hybrid membranes. Their therapeutic applications are critically evaluated, with a primary focus on cancer therapy, including photothermal and photodynamic approaches, alongside applications in cardiovascular, neurological, infectious, inflammatory, and regenerative diseases. Recent CM-NP platforms are systematically summarized according to membrane source, therapeutic cargo or nanoparticle core, disease application, and major outcomes, while recent patents are discussed to highlight emerging technological and translational developments. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, clinical translation remains constrained by challenges in membrane isolation and purification, batch reproducibility, manufacturing scalability, preservation of membrane integrity and functionality, quality control, long-term stability, biosafety, and regulatory standardization. Advances in membrane engineering, hybrid membrane systems, scalable manufacturing, standardized characterization, and rigorous safety evaluation will be important for advancing CM-NPs toward clinical translation.

articles.title: Gold Nanoparticle-Enabled Cancer Therapy: Translational Design Rules for Photothermal-Immunotherapy and Multimodal Precision Oncology.
articles.abstract: Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) are versatile cancer-therapy platforms with tunable plasmonic properties, high atomic number, accessible surface chemistry, and potential for integration into theranostic systems. By controlling size, morphology, surface composition, and cargo-loading strategies, AuNPs can support photothermal therapy (PTT), chemotherapy delivery, nucleic-acid transport, radiosensitization, photodynamic therapy (PDT), sonodynamic therapy (SDT), and image-guided treatment. Among these applications, AuNP-mediated PTT is particularly attractive because localized hyperthermia can induce tumor-cell injury, support controlled cargo release, and, under appropriate conditions, contribute to immunogenic cell death and remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. However, promising preclinical findings have not translated into widespread routine oncology practice. Major barriers include heterogeneous tumor accumulation, limited penetration beyond perivascular regions, mononuclear phagocyte system uptake, uncertain long-term biodistribution and clearance, inadequate manufacturing reproducibility, and incomplete safety standardization. The enhanced permeability and retention effect is variable across tumors, lesions, and patients; it should not be regarded as a universal basis for clinical nanoparticle delivery. This review summarizes the physicochemical design principles governing AuNP biological performance and critically evaluates their major therapeutic uses in oncology. Particular emphasis is placed on photothermal-immunotherapy, tumor-microenvironment modulation, multimodal synergy, and pharmacokinetic, toxicological, manufacturing, and regulatory barriers. We propose a translational framework connecting material quality attributes, route of administration and in vivo fate, local energy delivery and thermal dosimetry, immune activation, patient selection, and clinically meaningful endpoints. This framework may guide development of more reproducible, controllable, and clinically relevant AuNP cancer therapies.

articles.title: The Stability-Release Paradox in Long-Acting Peptide and Protein Delivery: A Review of Material-Cargo Compatibility and Therapeutic Integrity.
articles.abstract: Long-acting peptide and protein delivery requires more than prolonged release; the therapeutic must remain chemically, physically, structurally, and functionally competent throughout processing, depot residence, and release. This review examines the stability-release paradox, in which material features introduced to extend residence can also alter cargo integrity. Rather than cataloging platforms or restating the need for biologic stabilization, the literature is organized around a cargo-specific compatibility question: whether a retention mechanism, depot microenvironment, and intended residence time remain compatible with preservation of therapeutic attributes required for activity. Published experimental studies and recent reviews available through 10 August 2026 were critically examined, with emphasis on poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) systems, hydrogels, affinity-based depots, self-assembling formulations, and translational studies linking release with stability or pharmacological performance. Across these platforms, integrity is influenced by hydration, microclimate pH, reactive degradation products, drug-material affinity, interfacial exposure, local concentration, molecular crowding, processing stress, and host-depot interactions. Experimental studies of degradable polyesters show that prolonged mass release can coexist with peptide acylation or other chemical changes, whereas hydrogel and affinity systems demonstrate that reversible retention can suppress premature escape but still requires cargo-specific verification of recovery and biological function. The review therefore frames long-acting formulation design around three linked considerations: the depot as a dynamic pharmaceutical microenvironment, therapeutically competent release as an endpoint beyond cumulative mass recovery, and residence-time-stability matching as a compatibility test between planned confinement and the cargo's demonstrated stability window. This framework supports material selection and evaluation based on therapeutic integrity, stability-indicating release measurements, clinically relevant loading, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) evidence appropriate to the therapeutic claim.

articles.title: Functional Delivery of Nanoimmunotherapies in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Barrier-Informed Pharmaceutics Framework.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) presents a stringent drug-delivery environment in which tumor accumulation does not necessarily translate into target-cell exposure or cargo activity. This critical narrative review develops a barrier-informed framework for evaluating nanoimmunotherapies across systemic exposure, tumor access, target-cell delivery, cargo release, target engagement, and pharmacological activity. The framework links vascular, stromal, immune, metabolic, and intracellular barriers to cargo-carrier selection, administration route, biological identity, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and intracellular trafficking. Platforms discussed include nanovaccines and nucleic-acid therapeutics, engineered extracellular vesicles, nanoengineered oncolytic-virus delivery, nanoparticle-assisted immune-cell programming, checkpoint modulation, and stromal or metabolic strategies relevant to immune-directed therapy. Functional-delivery evidence is integrated with critical quality attributes, mechanism-based potency, manufacturing comparability, biosafety, repeat-dose performance, and biomarker-guided clinical development. We propose a qualitative stage-gating framework based on concordant evidence of target-site exposure, target-cell activity, reproducible product quality, acceptable repeat-dose performance, and a testable biomarker strategy. This framework supports formulation selection, cross-platform comparison, and translational prioritization of PDAC nanoimmunotherapies.

articles.title: From Target Discovery to Spatial Delivery: A Translational Roadmap for Gene-Targeted Therapies in Glioma.
articles.abstract: Diffuse gliomas are increasingly defined by molecular alterations, yet the clinical translation of gene-targeted therapies remains constrained by a persistent mismatch between target biology and spatial pharmacology. In this review, we connect target discovery to clinical development by integrating spatial and longitudinal tumor biology with payload selection, delivery engineering, biomarker design, manufacturing, and mechanism-driven trials. Recent clinical practices in locoregional CAR-T cells, oncolytic and gene-delivery viruses, tumor-homing myeloid cell gene therapy, mutation- and neoantigen-directed vaccination, RNA nanomedicines, and emerging genome-editing strategies suggest that vehicle and route of administration dramatically change drug exposure, therapeutic index, immune activity, and resistance. We therefore propose the concept of "delivery-adjusted targetability," in which a candidate target is judged not only by biological dependency but also by clonality, longitudinal stability, normal-brain expression, anatomical distribution, modality compatibility, and achievable target engagement. We further argue that the clinically actionable unit in diffuse glioma is often a target-anatomical compartment pair rather than a molecular target considered in isolation. Moreover, we advocate target-payload-vehicle-route-biomarker co-design and a stage-gated evidence package. This framework provides a potential way to compare otherwise dissimilar platforms, distinguish target failure from delivery failure, and reject biologically attractive but spatially implausible programs earlier. Treating molecular dependency and spatial access as a single design problem can make precision neuro-oncology more experimentally falsifiable and clinically actionable.

articles.title: Curcumin Nanodelivery for Tumor-Associated Macrophage Reprogramming and Immune-Checkpoint Sensitization: Engineering the Tumor Immune Microenvironment.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Curcumin possesses antineoplastic and immunomodulatory activities. However, poor aqueous solubility, chemical instability, rapid conjugative metabolism, and limited systemic exposure restrict meaningful concentrations within tumors. Numerous reviews have already addressed curcumin nanoformulations, improved bioavailability, and general anticancer effects. However, delivery architecture, cell-specific curcumin exposure, TAM functional reprogramming, macrophage-lymphocyte crosstalk, and checkpoint response remain insufficiently integrated. This review connects these components while distinguishing experimentally demonstrated links from mechanistic inference and examines whether engineered curcumin nanodelivery can remodel TAM-associated biology to improve responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1-directed therapy. Methods: A structured narrative review was conducted using experimental studies of curcumin delivery, macrophage targeting and reprogramming, intracellular signaling, macrophage-lymphocyte crosstalk, and checkpoint regulation. Results: Evidence supports curcumin-associated modulation of STAT3/STAT6, PI3K-AKT, context-dependent NF-κB, HIF-1α, redox, and metabolic pathways, accompanied by reduced immunosuppressive mediators and enhanced antitumor macrophage functions. Emerging nanoplatforms further report TAM remodeling, immunogenic cell death, enhanced T-cell responses, and additional therapeutic benefit in checkpoint-containing regimens. However, these endpoints are usually distributed across different experimental systems rather than one complete causal sequence. We therefore distinguish validated TAM targeting from tumor accumulation, biomimetic tumor homing, secondary TAM exposure, and combination benefit from demonstrated checkpoint sensitization. Conclusions: We propose a multidimensional D1-D8 evidence framework evaluating pharmaceutical performance, tumor exposure, TAM-specific uptake and intracellular parent curcumin, pathway modulation, functional TAM reprogramming, downstream immune restoration, checkpoint-therapy response, and translational relevance as independent domains. This prevents efficacy in one domain from being interpreted as proof of unmeasured links elsewhere and advances cell-resolved, mechanism-driven curcumin immunonanomedicine.

articles.title: Convergent Modifiers of Exposure Variability in Approved Cannabinoid Medicines: Pharmacogenomics, Drug-Drug Interactions, and Parent-Metabolite Divergence.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Systemic exposure to the approved cannabinoid medicines cannabidiol, nabiximols, dronabinol, and nabilone varies markedly among patients. Genotype and comedication may act at shared clearance steps and alter parent-drug and active-metabolite exposures differently. This review integrates pharmacogenomic, drug-drug interaction, and post-approval safety evidence within a convergent exposure-modifier (CEM) framework and develops testable hypotheses about their joint effects. Methods: A narrative, integrative review of bibliographic databases and regulatory documents for these medicines and key co-medications. Evidence was synthesized by pathway, product, analyte, interaction direction, directness, actionability, and limitations. Results: The framework distinguishes a victim branch, in which genotype and comedication modify cannabinoid exposure, from a perpetrator branch, in which cannabinoids alter co-medication exposure, with genotype potentially modifying it. Component evidence is strongest at CYP2C19 (cannabidiol-clobazam) and CYP2C9 (THC-containing medicines): cannabidiol increased N-desmethylclobazam exposure 3.4-fold in healthy volunteers while parent clobazam changed little, and CYP2C19 poor-metabolizer status independently increases baseline metabolite exposure. Comedication may phenoconvert genotype-predicted activity. No approved-product study identified in this review measured the joint genotype-by-comedication effect. Framework maturity is uneven: the predictions are cannabidiol-anchored; one relies on oral Δ9-THC evidence of unspecified formulation; nabiximols generates none, lacking genotype-stratified pharmacokinetics; and nabilone is excluded because its active-metabolite contributions are uncharacterized, although parent-drug activity is established. Conclusions: CEM is hypothesis-generating, not tested here: the three core predictions are falsifiable genotype-by-treatment tests requiring prospective validation. Label- and study-supported monitoring stands on its own evidence; the framework's predictions do not, and genotype-guided dosing remains unvalidated.

articles.title: Unraveling Vulnerabilities and Pathways Responsible for AITL Malignancy to Improve Patients' Treatment.
articles.abstract: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) is an aggressive subtype of peripheral T-cell lymphoma characterized by poor clinical outcomes following conventional CHOP-based chemotherapy and the lack of effective disease-specific therapeutic options. The disease finds its origin in CD4 follicular helper T (Tfh) cells and is driven by recurrent genetic alterations, including mutations in TET2, RHOA, DNMT3A, and IDH2. Despite the rarity of AITL, preclinical models have been fundamental in elucidating disease pathogenesis, identifying key molecular vulnerabilities and providing platforms for the evaluation of novel therapeutic strategies. These studies have highlighted multiple targetable pathways, including aberrant mTOR, T-cell receptor and NF-κB signaling. Additionally, widespread epigenetic alterations in the neoplastic T-cells were uncovered due to mutations in epigenetic modifiers in AITL. More recently, metabolic reprogramming has emerged as an additional therapeutic vulnerability, revealing a strong dependence of AITL cells on mitochondrial respiration and lipid metabolism, particularly the choline metabolic pathway. Advances in the understanding of AITL biology have also accelerated the development of immunotherapeutic strategies. Monoclonal antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, immune checkpoint inhibitors and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies have shown encouraging preclinical and early clinical activity. Of note, the first preclinical results on an in vivo CAR-T-cell approach for AITL are reported. Here we provide a broad overview of AITL, discussing its biological features, pathogenesis, preclinical models, current treatment landscape, and recent advances in therapeutic approaches.

articles.title: Nanoenzyme-Enhanced Catalytic Photodynamic Therapy for Cancer.
articles.abstract: Catalytic photodynamic therapy is an emerging strategy that integrates enzyme-mimetic nanomaterials with photosensitisers to overcome the intrinsic limitations of conventional photodynamic therapy in solid tumours. Conventional photodynamic therapy relies on the oxygen-dependent generation of cytotoxic reactive oxygen species, which is severely compromised by tumour hypoxia, elevated antioxidant defences, heterogenous photosensitiser accumulation, and limited light penetration. Nanoenzyme-mediated catalytic photodynamic therapy addresses these barriers through two mechanistically distinct catalytic modes: oxygen-generating catalytic photodynamic therapy, in which catalase-like nanoenzymes disproportionate endogenous hydrogen peroxide into molecular oxygen to sustain Type II photochemistry, and oxygen-independent catalytic photodynamic therapy, in which peroxidase/Fenton-like nanoenzymes convert hydrogen peroxide into hydroxyl radicals without requiring oxygen or light activation. Multi-enzyme cascade systems integrate both modes, enabling synergistic reactive oxygen species generation across heterogenous tumour regions. This review discusses the catalytic mechanisms, nanoenzyme classes, including carbon-based materials, metal-organic frameworks, plasmonic nanostructures, and biomimetic systems, and therapeutic applications of catalytic photodynamic therapy. We critically evaluate the evidence linking catalytic activity to improved photodynamic outcomes, highlight methodological limitations in reactive oxygen species assessment, and examine translational challenges including substrate heterogeneity, colloidal scalability, uncontrolled reactive oxygen species generation, and regulatory hurdles. Emerging research directions, including artificial intelligence-mediated nanomaterial design, quantum-guided catalytic optimisation, and immunoengineering, are considered as strategies to accelerate clinical translation.

articles.title: Emerging Technologies in Granulation: Process Analytical Technologies and Modeling Approaches in Pharmaceutical Development and Manufacturing.
articles.abstract: In the present review, 32 studies, published between 2020 and 2026, were reviewed to identify recent advances in pharmaceutical granulation. Emphasis is placed on the integration of real-time monitoring technologies, recent Process Analytical Technologies (PATs) approaches, the relationships between critical process parameters (CPPs) and critical quality attributes (CQAs) affecting the product, and continuous manufacturing, as well as the implementation of modern data processing models. Increased attention was paid to continuous granulation using twin-screw extrusion, alongside the use of spectroscopic technologies for monitoring the production continuum. Finally, novel modeling approaches are discussed, revealing a transition from solely empirical methods toward hybrid models that combine data analysis tools with mechanistic process understanding and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven applications, yielding a new era with the transformation of both batch and continuous manufacturing. The study highlights the integration of PATs, modeling and QbD to enhance process understanding and control, but also challenges from a regulatory framework perspective that resulting from these technological advancements.

articles.title: Progress in Anti-Obesity Drug Development: A Pharmacodynamics Perspective.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Obesity is a chronic, multifactorial condition driven by complex neuroendocrine and metabolic pathways that limit the long-term success of lifestyle interventions. Pharmacotherapy has advanced from early monoaminergic agents to incretin-based and multi-receptor agonists with substantially improved efficacy. This review aims to provide pharmacodynamics-focused synthesis of current and emerging anti-obesity medications, emphasizing mechanistic targets, receptor interactions, and translational implications. Methods: We conducted a narrative review integrating Phase I-III clinical trials, mechanistic pharmacology data (receptor affinity, potency, and signaling bias), and regulatory summaries for FDA-approved and selected emerging, investigational, repurposed, or regionally approved anti-obesity agents. Inclusion focused on clinical relevance, pharmacodynamic novelty, and weight-loss efficacy. Results: Approved anti-obesity medications act through diverse pathways, including the inhibition of fat absorption (orlistat), the modulation of central appetite circuits (phentermine/topiramate, naltrexone/bupropion), and incretin-based mechanisms (liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, and the oral GLP-1 receptor agonists semaglutide 25 mg and the nonpeptide orforglipron). GLP-1 receptor agonists achieve approximately 6-15% weight loss, while dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists such as tirzepatide reach 15-20%. Emerging agents-including triple agonists (retatrutide), glucagon-based co-agonists, amylin analogs with Phase III efficacy data, earlier-stage growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) pathway agonists, and peripherally restricted cannabinoid-1 receptor inverse agonists-demonstrate enhanced metabolic effects and potential improvements in lean-mass preservation. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics highlight the need for individualized dosing strategies. Conclusions: Clinical efficacy and tolerability cannot be inferred from receptor identity alone. They emerge from relative receptor potency and efficacy, exposure, tissue access, receptor trafficking, and mechanism-linked adverse effects. Dual and triple agonists can broaden efficacy, but receptor balance and standardized comparative pharmacology remain essential for rational development and individualized dosing.

articles.title: Retatrutide as a Unimolecular GIP/GLP-1/Glucagon Receptor Tri-Agonist: Molecular Design, Pharmaceutical Development and Critical Interpretation of Emerging Phase 3 Evidence.
articles.abstract: Retatrutide (LY3437943) is an investigational, once-weekly, lipidated 39-residue peptide that activates the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide-1, and glucagon receptors. Its molecular design combines incretin activity with glucagon receptor engagement while maintaining glycaemic efficacy. This critical narrative review examines molecular engineering, pharmacokinetics, dose escalation, pharmaceutical development, and clinical evidence available through 11 September 2026. Five phase 3 trials have reported positive primary outcomes, but only TRANSCEND-T2D-1 has a full peer-reviewed report; the obesity trials are currently available as sponsor topline disclosures. In those disclosures, efficacy-estimand mean weight reductions of 28.3% at 80 weeks (TRIUMPH-1) and 28.7% at 68 weeks (TRIUMPH-4) were reported, with a TRIUMPH-1 treatment-regimen estimate of 25.0%; these values remain provisional pending full published trial reports. The peer-reviewed TRANSCEND-T2D-1 report supports glycaemic efficacy in early type 2 diabetes. Interpretation requires attention to estimands, population differences, treatment discontinuation and selection into trial extensions. Gastrointestinal adverse events, dysaesthesia, heart-rate changes and the functional consequences of lean-mass loss require further evaluation. Pharmaceutical priorities include scalable synthesis, impurity and potency control, formulation stability, immunogenicity and reliable dose delivery. Retatrutide provides a clinically advanced example of unimolecular poly-agonism, but comparative effectiveness, long-term outcomes and regulatory review remain essential to defining its therapeutic role.
