Following treatment with alfuzosin and doxazosin, both drugs significantly induced apoptosis, with total apoptotic populations reaching 39.48% and 35.61%, respectively, compared with only 2.77% in untreated MCF-7 cells. Molecular docking studies further indicated the ability to interact with key amino acids within the EGFR active site. Conclusions: The present findings demonstrate the potential repurposing of alfuzosin and doxazosin as anticancer agents and offer a good background for further mechanistic and in vivo investigations.

articles.title: Changes in Adrenergic and Cholinergic Receptors on Human Cerebral Vessels.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sporadic cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) occurs due to a failure of clearance of amyloid-beta (Aβ) along the walls of capillaries and arteries. Soluble Aβ is eliminated from the brain along the basement membranes of capillaries and arteries as Intramural Periarterial Drainage (IPAD). The motive force for IPAD is provided by the spontaneous contractions of vascular smooth muscle cells, as vasomotion. Cerebrovascular smooth muscle cells receive adrenergic and cholinergic innervation from the Locus Coeruleus and the Nucleus Basalis of Meynert, which are compromised very early in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Here, we tested the hypothesis that adrenergic and cholinergic receptors are histologically preserved in parenchymal and leptomeningeal blood vessels with CAA. Methods: Using immunohistochemistry, we examined the cerebrovascular distribution of muscarinic (M1, M2), nicotinic (α 7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor), and adrenergic (α1b/2b) receptors in post-mortem brain tissue. We compared receptor distribution across CAA and non-CAA patients, as well as young and old patients without CAA. Results: We found significant differences in the receptor immunoreactivity of α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as well as α1b and α2b adrenergic receptors. However, there were no differences in the receptor immunoreactivity of M1 or M2 muscarinic receptors between patient groups. Conclusions: As IPAD depends on the functionality of the vascular smooth muscle cells to maintain the integrity of IPAD with aging, based on these histological findings, future therapeutic interventions could focus on agonists of α7 nicotinic acetylcholine and α1b/2b adrenergic receptors.

articles.title: Nanocarrier System Based on Jabuticaba Peel Co-Products and Caffeine for Photoprotective and Regenerative Skin Applications.
articles.abstract: Background: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, urban pollution and depletion of cutaneous antioxidant reserves are interconnected drivers of photoaging, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activation, mitochondrial dysfunction and dermal extracellular matrix degradation. Plant polyphenols can counteract these processes, but topical efficacy is limited by chemical instability, polarity-driven partitioning and a hostile stratum corneum delivery interface. Here we report a green nanostructured lipid carrier co-loading a phenolic-rich jabuticaba (Plinia cauliflora) peel extract and caffeine (NLC-JC), engineered with Amazonian lipids (Astrocaryum murumuru butter and Orbignya phalerata oil) and stabilized by a Natural Deep Eutectic Solvent (NaDES)-like microenvironment. Methods: UPLC profiling was used to determine the polyphenolic composition of the extract. Physicochemical characterization included hydrodynamic diameter and PDI, ζ-potential, lipid matrix organization (XRD) and morphology (TEM), as well as colloidal stability over 30 days. Cytotoxicity was assessed in SH-4 melanocytes (ISO 10993-5) and in zebrafish (Danio rerio) embryos (96-h IC50, GHS acute hazard threshold). Functional antioxidant and photoprotective activity was evaluated by DPPH radical scavenging, and by attenuation of UVC- and H2O2-induced anion superoxide generation, alongside assessment of cellular and nuclear morphology under combined oxidative stress. Results: UPLC profiling revealed a polyphenolic fingerprint dominated by ellagic acid (476.8 ± 19.7 µg g-1), quercetin-3-rhamnoside (90.9 ± 4.6 µg g-1), quercetin (83.7 ± 1.4 µg g-1), cyanidin-3-glucoside (73.0 ± 1.2 µg g-1) and protocatechuic acid (68.2 ± 2.2 µg g-1), bioactives with documented anti-MMP, NF-κB-suppressing and ROS-scavenging activities. Optimized NLC-JC showed a hydrodynamic diameter of 56.1 nm (PDI = 0.131), negative ζ-potential, amorphous lipid matrix (XRD) and spherical morphology (TEM, ≈150-200 nm electron-dense particles), with 30-day colloidal stability. NLC-JC exhibited low cytotoxicity in SH-4 melanocytes (IC50 = 2304 μg mL-1), preserving ≥70% viability across the cosmetically relevant range (ISO 10993-5), and a 96-h LC50 of 2013 μg mL-1 in zebrafish (Danio rerio) embryos, three orders of magnitude above the GHS acute hazard threshold (100 mg L-1). Functionally, NLC-JC produced ≈50% DPPH radical scavenging at concentrations comparable to ascorbic acid, attenuated UVC- and H2O2-induced anion superoxide generation and preserved cellular and nuclear morphology under combined oxidative stress. Conclusion: These data position NLC-JC as a safe-by-design, multifunctional dermocosmetic platform combining agro-industrial valorization with mechanism-anchored photoprotection.

articles.title: In Vitro Antileishmanial Activity and Cytotoxicity Evaluation of 2-(Thiophen-2-ylmethyl)quinazolin-4(3H)-one Derivatives Against Leishmania tropica and Leishmania infantum.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease and the toxicity, limited efficacy and emerging drug resistance of current therapies underscore the urgent need for new antileishmanial agents. This study aimed to experimentally assess the in vitro antileishmanial activity, cytotoxicity and selectivity of quinazolin-4(3H)-one derivatives against Leishmania tropica and Leishmania infantum and to computationally investigate the potential interaction of compound E9 with trypanothione reductase. Methods: The in vitro antileishmanial activities of sixteen quinazolin-4(3H)-one derivatives (E1-E16) against the promastigote forms of L. tropica and L. infantum were evaluated. Additionally, the most active compounds were subjected to an evaluation of their cytotoxicity in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and their selectivity indices (SIs) were subsequently calculated. Molecular docking and molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA) analyses were performed for compound E9 against L. infantum trypanothione reductase. Results: Compounds E2, E9 and E11 showed activity against L. tropica, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 23.2, 22.4 and 76.0 μM, respectively. In contrast, compounds E2, E3, E9 and E11 were active against L. infantum, with IC50 values of 38.1, 69.7, 28.2 and 86.7 μM, respectively, suggesting species-dependent activity. Furthermore, among the tested compounds, E2 showed the most favorable selectivity profile against L. tropica and L. infantum, with SI values of 8.8 and 5.4, respectively. Moreover, molecular docking of E9 produced a docking score of -8.070 kcal/mol, with MM/GBSA analysis indicating a binding free energy of -82.44 kcal/mol. Conclusions: These findings support further investigation of quinazolin-4(3H)-one derivatives as potential antileishmanial agents, with E2 emerging as the most selective compound. Furthermore, they suggest that the biological activity of this compound series may differ among Leishmania species. The molecular modeling findings suggest a potential interaction between E9 and trypanothione reductase, supporting the need for further evaluation of these compounds in intracellular amastigote models and subsequent in vivo studies.

articles.title: Ocrelizumab-Induced Leukocyte Subpopulations Dynamics in Multiple Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease of the CNS characterized by immune-mediated inflammation and neurodegeneration. Based on its immunoablative effect targeting the CD20-positive B lymphocytes, ocrelizumab has emerged as a valid therapeutic option for MS. Although the on-treatment dynamics of leukocyte subpopulations are crucial for optimizing therapeutic strategies, little data are available in this field. Here, we aim to investigate how pre- and post-infusion immune-cell subsets change and correlate with each other, and how CD19+ B cell repopulation evolves over time. Methods: In an observational, retrospective, and prospective real-world study, we studied 51 relapsing-remitting MS ocrelizumab-treated patients who underwent flow cytometric immunophenotyping before and after each infusion and at three-month intervals, up to the eighth (4 years), for a total of 408 cycles. Results: After an initial decrease, post-infusion lymphocyte count returned to normal, while total white blood cells showed a sawtooth pattern driven by post-infusion increases. Granulocytes and natural killer cell counts remained substantially stable, while monocytes showed a significant cyclic pattern: increasing post-infusion, decreasing at the intermediate time point, with a more pronounced reduction pre-infusion, and rising again after re-administration. CD3+ and CD4+ T cells exhibited the same cyclic sawtooth pattern observed for monocytes. The CD4+/CD8+ ratio progressively increased, reflecting a significant elevation of CD4+, CD3+ and, to a lesser extent, CD8+ T cells. Pre-infusion CD19+ B cell counts progressively decreased, approaching zero by the fourth treatment year. Pre-treatment CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, lymphocyte, monocyte, and granulocyte counts differed significantly from on-treatment values. Correlation analyses showed that the major relationships among leukocyte subsets remained preserved throughout treatment. Conclusions: This study details leukocyte subpopulation dynamics during ocrelizumab therapy, unveiling previously unrecognized immunomodulatory properties beyond B-cell depletion. Ocrelizumab predominantly affects adaptive immunity, with potential indirect effects on innate immune compartments, and is associated with changes across immune-cell populations. These findings could have implications for individualized treatment strategies, but their direct application in this field still requires confirmatory studies on immunophenotyping and peripheral B-cell repopulation dynamics.

articles.title: Sophocarpine Inhibits Proliferation and Triggers Apoptosis in Breast Cancer Cells by Modulating the miR-21/PTEN/AKT and ERK1/2 Signaling Networks.
articles.abstract: Background: Sophocarpine (SC), a tetracyclic quinolizidine alkaloid, has shown antitumor potential, yet its activity and underlying mechanisms in breast cancer remain unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the anticancer effects of SC and the molecular mechanism, focusing on the involvement of microRNA-21 (miR-21) and AKT/mTOR and ERK1/2 signaling networks. Methods: In MDA-MB-231 and T-47D breast cancer cells, SC cytotoxicity and growth-inhibitory effects were evaluated using MTT viability, colony formation, migration assays, and flow cytometry for cell cycle and apoptosis analysis. RT-qPCR analysis, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining were performed to measure RNA and protein expression, respectively. Molecular docking analysis was performed to explore SC's interaction with the miR-21 precursor. Results: SC treatment effectively inhibited the proliferation, survival, and migration of breast cancer cells. It also induced cell cycle arrest and triggered apoptosis in both cell lines. Mechanistically, SC downregulated oncogenic miR-21 transcription, thereby enhancing tumor suppressors PTEN and PDCD4 and suppressing AKT/mTOR and ERK1/2 signaling. Interestingly, restoration of miR-21 reversed SC's effects on PTEN and PDCD4, confirming SC's miR-21 dependency. Docking analysis suggested that SC may bind the miR-21 precursor and interfere with its maturation. SC also increased long noncoding RNA GAS5 while reducing miR-196a-5p and HIF-1α transcripts. It shifted the Bcl2/Bax/Bad/caspases balance toward apoptosis. Conclusions: These findings identify SC as a potential structural scaffold exhibiting preliminary anti-tumor activity against breast cancer cells, at least in part, through modulating miR-21 and inhibition of the AKT/mTOR/ERK1/2 survival network.

articles.title: Comparative Network Pharmacology and Molecular Docking Analysis of Ursodeoxycholic Acid and Tauroursodeoxycholic Acid in Alzheimer's Disease-Associated Molecular Networks.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid- and tau-related pathology, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysregulation, and neuronal loss. Previous studies have shown the potential effects of bile acids, especially ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), on neurodegenerative diseases. However, whether UDCA and TUDCA exhibit distinct molecular interaction patterns within an Alzheimer's disease-associated biological context remains unclear. This study aims to compare the relevant targets, enrichment pathways, and docking profiles predicted by UDCA and TUDCA using the computer network pharmacology framework. Methods: The study combined analysis of networks relating to drug action with methods examining how structures bind. We predicted potential targets of UDCA and TUDCA by using public databases and intersected with AD-related genes. Protein-protein interaction network construction, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyses, and integrated compound-target-pathway network analysis were performed. Key targets were further evaluated by molecular docking to characterize predicted binding patterns and ligand-target interaction profiles. Results: UDCA and TUDCA share 98 and 103 intersecting genes with AD, respectively, with significant overlapping targets. Functional enrichment analysis showed that UDCA-related targets were significantly enriched in nuclear receptor activity, transcriptional regulation, and metabolic pathways. TUDCA-related targets are more significantly enriched in cell survival, kinase activity and neural activity ligand-receptor interactions. Molecular docking analyses provided target-specific structural information, while same-target docking using GPBAR1 and MAPK14 further revealed ligand-dependent differences in predicted interaction patterns under identical receptor conditions. Results from approaches examining systems and structure both indicate that ursodeoxycholic acid and tauroursodeoxycholic acid show profiles of action that work together. UDCA was associated with predicted upstream regulatory and metabolic-related target profiles, whereas TUDCA showed greater association with intracellular signaling, apoptosis-related, and neuronal survival-related pathways. Conclusions: The two bile acids showed predicted associations with pathways related to cell death regulation, inflammation, and metabolism. These findings provide a methodological basis and testable hypotheses for future experimental validation, but they should not be interpreted as direct evidence of therapeutic efficacy in Alzheimer's disease.

articles.title: Topical Application of Derris scandens Gel for Musculoskeletal Pain Relief and Enhanced Fitness Performance: A Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is a common and recurrent symptom in athletes following intensive or eccentric exercise. This study evaluated the efficacy of a topical gel of Derris scandens stem extract on pain and countermovement jump (CMJ) performance in athletes with exercise-induced DOMS and assessed skin irritation in healthy volunteers. Methods: Genistein-7-O-[α-rhamnosyl-(1→6)-β-glucopyranoside] (GG), a chemical marker of D. scandens, was quantified by HPLC. In a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial, athletes applied D. scandens gel (5%) or diclofenac gel (1%) to the painful site twice daily for 7 days. Pain was recorded daily using a visual analog scale, and CMJ was evaluated on days 1, 2, 4, and 8. Changes from the pre-treatment assessment were compared between groups. Results:D. scandens gel caused no skin irritation in healthy volunteers. Twenty-five athletes completed the trial (D. scandens, n = 13; diclofenac, n = 12). Pain scores decreased and CMJ recovered over the treatment period in both groups, with a significant effect of time but no significant treatment-by-time interaction or treatment effect. Pain reduction from day 2 to day 8 did not differ between groups (MD, 1.75; 95% CI, -1.01 to 4.51; p = 0.203), nor did CMJ recovery (MD, 1.96 cm; 95% CI, -2.01 to 5.93; p = 0.315). No adverse events were reported. Conclusions: Topical D. scandens gel was well tolerated, and both treatment groups showed reductions in DOMS-related pain and recovery of CMJ performance over the treatment period. Between-group differences were not statistically significant. Trial registration: Thai Clinical Trials Registry TCTR20180608003.

articles.title: Association of Vitamin D Supplementation with VDR and CAMP Expression and Ulcer Healing in Diabetic Foot Infection Involving Biofilm-Forming Bacteria: An Exploratory Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Diabetic foot infections (DFIs) are a major cause of morbidity and lower-limb amputation. Vitamin D exerts immunomodulatory effects through vitamin D receptor (VDR), which regulates the cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (CAMP) gene that encodes cathelicidin (LL-37). However, their association with DFIs remains poorly understood. This study investigated the association between vitamin D supplementation, the vitamin D-VDR-CAMP-LL-37 pathway, and ulcer healing in DFIs involving biofilm-forming bacteria. Methods: This study (September 2022-March 2026) included 16 DFI patients in the study group (SG), 16 in the reference group (RG), and 16 healthy controls (HCs). The SG received vitamin D supplementation (60,000 IU) in addition to standard care, whereas the RG received standard care alone. Participants were followed up for 4 months. Vitamin D assessment (electrochemiluminescence immunoassay), VDR and LL-37 quantification (ELISA), biofilm formation (tissue culture plate method), and VDR and CAMP gene expression (mRNA quantitation) were all considered. Results: At baseline, serum vitamin D, VDR protein, and LL-37 levels differed significantly among the groups (p ≤ 0.002), whereas VDR and CAMP gene expressions did not. Following supplementation, the SG showed significant increases in serum vitamin D, VDR protein and LL-37 (p ≤ 0.001). At the four-month follow-up, there was no significant difference in VDR and CAMP gene expression or in ulcer healing between the groups. Although a higher proportion of participants in the SG achieved ulcer healing, the difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Although changes in the circulating elements of the vitamin D-VDR-LL-37 pathway were noted with physician-prescribed vitamin D supplementation, no statistically significant association with ulcer healing was observed. This finding requires validation through a thorough investigation.

articles.title: Protective Effects of Total Alkaloids of Rhizoma Corydalis Against Neuronal Ferroptosis Through a PPARγ-Dependent Mechanism in Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Impairment.
articles.abstract: Objectives: Previous studies from our laboratory have established a strong correlation between diabetes-associated cognitive impairment (DACI) and neuronal ferroptosis. This study aimed to elucidate the therapeutic mechanisms of total alkaloids of rhizoma corydalis (TAC) in mitigating DACI, with a specific focus on its modulation of neuronal ferroptosis via the PPARγ pathway. Methods: Therapeutic targets were predicted utilizing bioinformatics, molecular docking, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses. In vivo, a DACI rat model was established via a high-fat/high-sugar diet coupled with streptozotocin (STZ) intraperitoneal injection, followed by TAC administration. In vitro, HT22 cell injury was induced by palmitic acid and high glucose (PA + HG) exposure. Small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated PPARγ knockdown was employed to validate the protective mechanisms of TAC. Results: Multi-omics and computational analyses identified neuronal PPARγ as the central target mediating the anti-ferroptotic effects of TAC. In vivo assessments demonstrated that TAC administration significantly attenuated spatial memory deficits, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance in diabetic rats. Furthermore, TAC mitigated hippocampal neuronal injury and mitochondrial morphological abnormalities, decreased iron overload and lipid peroxidation, and normalized the expression profiles of ferroptosis-associated proteins. In vitro assays, corroborated by siRNA-mediated knockdown, confirmed that TAC specifically upregulates PPARγ, which subsequently activates the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling axis and enhances GPX4 expression, ultimately conferring resistance against neuronal ferroptosis. Conclusions: TAC emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for DACI, exerting its neuroprotective efficacy intrinsically through the targeted activation of PPARγ to abrogate neuronal ferroptosis.

articles.title: Predicting Chemotherapy Response in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: The Role of CYP2Cs as a Biomarker and a Drug Target (A Proof-of-Concept Study).
articles.abstract: Background: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) has a poor prognosis and limited targeted therapies, with anthracyclines being key treatments. However, many patients show reduced responsiveness to these treatments, affecting their outcomes. Arachidonic acid metabolites, specifically epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs) produced by cytochrome P450 (CYP) epoxygenase enzymes, have been implicated in TNBC progression. However, limited data exist on the role of CYP epoxygenase gene expression in the responsiveness of anthracycline-based therapy in TNBC. Thus, we aimed to test the contribution of these CYPs in anthracycline responsiveness among patients with TNBC and to explore whether inhibition of CYP epoxygenase can potentiate the anti-cancer activity of anthracyclines. Methods: Our study used the KM-plotter database to retrieve and extract patients' data with TNBC. The patients were assigned to two cohorts: responders or less-responders to anthracycline based on relapse-free survival. Additionally, the effects of the CYP epoxygenase inhibitor MSPPOH in combination with doxorubicin were evaluated in the TNBC cell line. Results: The present study shows that TNBC patients with lower responsiveness to anthracycline-based therapy exhibited higher levels of CYP2C8, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19. We also found that these CYP2Cs could be potential biomarkers for predicting anthracycline responsiveness. Using human TNBC cells, we show that a selective CYP2C epoxygenase inhibitor, MSPPOH, significantly potentiates the anti-cancer effect of anthracycline. Conclusions: Collectively, this study provides preliminary evidence that CYP2C epoxygenase is involved in the therapeutic response to anthracyclines in TNBC, suggesting that these enzymes may serve as predictive biomarkers. However, given the limitations of using a public database and a single TNBC cell line, continued validation within larger, independent patient cohorts is needed.

articles.title: Efficacy and Pharmacokinetics of Guanidine Derivative LQOF-G2 in an In Vivo Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis Model.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Due to their toxicity and the limited efficacy of current therapies, Leishmaniases represent a major public health challenge. The search for new treatments is urgent. LQOF-G2 is a synthetic guanidine compound whose in vitro leishmanicidal potential has already been investigated by our group. The present study evaluates the in vivo efficacy, safety-related parameters, treatment-associated cytokine responses, and pharmacokinetic (PK) properties of the novel guanidine derivative LQOF-G2. Methods: Golden hamsters infected with Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis were treated with LQOF-G2 (5 and 10 mg/kg, i.p.). Pharmacokinetic characterization was performed in BALB/c mice following intravenous and intraperitoneal administration. Results: Treatment with LQOF-G2 significantly reduced cutaneous lesion size and parasite burden at both the site of infection (up to 98.6 ± 0.8%) and in the lymph nodes (up to 99.7 ± 0.3%). No marked alterations were observed in the biochemical and hematological parameters evaluated at the tested doses. Treatment was associated with increased TNF-α and IFN-γ responses and reduced IL-10 levels following ex vivo antigen stimulation, consistent with a more pro-inflammatory/type-1-associated cytokine profile. Because murine cytokine ELISA reagents were used with golden hamster samples without independent species-specific analytical validation, these findings were considered exploratory and supportive rather than quantitatively validated evidence of an immunomodulatory mechanism. Pharmacokinetic characterization in BALB/c mice revealed moderate clearance (46 ± 4 mL/min/kg), a relatively large apparent volume of distribution (Vdss = 11 ± 1 L/kg), and a long elimination half-life (6.8 ± 0.4 h) following intravenous administration. After intraperitoneal administration, rapid absorption (Tmax = 0.25 h) and an absolute bioavailability of 44% were observed. Conclusions: Overall, these findings support LQOF-G2 as a candidate for further preclinical investigation in cutaneous leishmaniasis.

articles.title: Population-Specific Pharmacogenetic Variants Associated with Chemotherapy Response in the Bulgarian Population.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pharmacogenetic variability influences the efficacy and toxicity of anticancer therapies. However, Eastern European populations remain underrepresented in pharmacogenetic databases. This study aimed to characterize pharmacogenetic variants relevant to chemotherapy response in the Bulgarian population and compare their allele frequencies with reference populations. Methods: Ninety individuals were included, comprising 50 patients with colorectal, non-small cell lung, or breast cancer and 40 healthy controls. Genomic DNA and circulating cell-free DNA were analyzed by next-generation sequencing targeting pharmacogenetic genes involved in drug metabolism, transport, and DNA repair. Allele frequencies were compared with gnomAD v2.1.1 reference data. Sensitivity analyses compared Bulgarian controls with Bulgarian non-cancer and combined Southern European, Northwestern European, and Other non-Finnish European non-cancer populations. Results: Twenty-three pharmacogenetic variants were evaluated. Six variants remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction in both Fisher's exact test and the two-proportion Z-test. Five variants-DPYD c.2194G>A, XPC c.2815C>A, EGFR c.1562G>A, XRCC1 c.1196A>G, and ERCC2 c.2251A>C-showed higher allele frequencies, whereas ERCC2 c.934G>A was less frequent in the Bulgarian cohort. DPYD c.85T>C remained significant after correction in the Z-test but not in Fisher's exact test. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the significance of XPC c.2815C>A in both reference-population comparisons, while DPYD c.85T>C remained significant only against the combined European reference population. Conclusions: Several pharmacogenetic variants showed distinct allele frequencies in the Bulgarian cohort. XPC c.2815C>A demonstrated the most robust population-specific pattern across sensitivity analyses. These findings highlight the value of locally derived pharmacogenetic data for precision oncology and pharmacogenetically guided treatment strategies.

articles.title: Synthesis of Antiproliferative N-Chalconyl Imidazolidones and Mechanistic Evaluation of Prototype N-CIMZ 1 as a Macrophage-Modulating Antimitotic Agent.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: To address current aggressive breast cancer challenges, a novel series of eight N-chalconyl imidazolidone derivatives (N-CIMZs 1-8) was synthesized and evaluated for direct cytotoxicity and immunomodulation via macrophage polarization. Methods: Following antiproliferative screening against four representative breast cancer lines, the prototype candidate N-CIMZ 1 was selected for cell cycle and scratch-wound healing assays in MCF-7 cells. Multi-parametric flow cytometry on human THP-1 macrophages tracked cellular stress (γH2AX), metabolic markers (iNOS), and surface dynamics (LAP (TGF-β1), CD163, CD206, CD209). Results:N-CIMZ 1 acted as an antimitotic agent, inducing G2/M phase arrest (51.0%) and restricting MCF-7 wound confluence to 33% at 24 h. In THP-1 macrophages, it maintained low induction of γH2AX-mediated DNA damage signaling. Under alternative M2 pressure, N-CIMZ 1 intercepted polarization by forcing high membrane retention of the immunosuppressive peptide LAP (81%) and suppressing the scavenger marker CD163 (12%) while buffering hyper-reactive CD206+/CD209+ hybrid spikes down to 2.33% under M1 stress. Conclusions:N-CIMZ 1 represents a promising multi-modal scaffold combining antimitotic and macrophage-modulating properties. This targeted immunomodulation effectively subverts tumor-supportive macrophage phenotypes, showcasing the potential of microenvironment reprogramming to counter breast cancer progression and metastasis.

articles.title: In Vitro Antibacterial Potentials of Cinnamomum verum J. Presl (Cinnamon), Citrus x aurantium L. (Petitgrain) Pelargonium graveolens L'Hér (Rose Geranium), and Thymus vulgaris L. (Thyme) Essential Oil-Containing Ointments Against Canine Otitis Externa Pseudomonas aeruginosa Isolates.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Otitis externa is a common infection in dogs. The most important aetiological agent is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and an increasing number of cases are proving difficult to treat due to this pathogen's antibiotic resistance. Methods: We determined the composition of cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum J. Presl), petitgrain (Citrus x aurantium L.), rose geranium (Pelargonium graveolens L'Hér), and thyme (Thymus vulgaris L.) essential oils (EOs) using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). We then used the bioautographic method to identify antibacterial components. Two-and-a-half- and five percent concentrations of the essential oils were added to four different ointment bases, such as hydrogelum methylcellulose, unguentum oleosum, unguentum stearini, and vaselinum cholesterinatum, and the in vitro antibacterial effects were tested on lawns of six P. aeruginosa isolates using the antibiotic-containing product Marbogen complex as a control. The keepability of the methylcellulose-based ointments was monitored at 4 °C and 27 °C for 12 months, with efficacy losses evaluated monthly. Results: Hydrogel methylcellulose (HM) was the most effective at supporting the therapeutic efficacy of each oil, reducing the bacterial count on the exposed area by 99.999%, 100%, 100%, and 100% in the case of 5% cinnamon, petitgrain, rose geranium, and thyme, respectively. EO-based HM ointments take effect within 15 min, with only slight improvement after 30, 45, and 60 min. Cinnamon was the most effective when applied in the HM matrix. In contrast to the HM and US gel matrices, the antibacterial supportive effects of Unguentum oleosum and Vazelinum cholestrinatum were drastically lower. The antimicrobial efficacy of essential oils in hydrogel formulation varied significantly depending on the type of oil (p < 0.001), its concentration (p < 0.001), the exposure time (p < 0.001), and the P. aeruginosa isolate used (p < 0.001). Cinnamon oil demonstrated the highest efficacy, achieving near-complete bacterial elimination across all isolates within 15 min. There was no significant difference between the 2.5% and 5% concentrations (EMM: 0.016 vs. 0.004; p = 0.904). Conclusions: Our results demonstrate that essential oil-based products can be effective alternatives to antibiotics when used in conjunction with an effective gel matrix.

articles.title: Effect of Crosslinking on the Properties and Stability of Andrographolide Solid Dispersions.
articles.abstract: Objectives: Crosslinking enhances solid dispersion (SD) stability but often restricts drug release, and this trade-off remains unresolved. In this study, crosslinked polyvinyl alcohol-suberic acid ester (CPSE) carriers with different crosslinking degrees were prepared to investigate the effects of crosslinking on the properties, dissolution and stability of andrographolide (AG)-SDs, aiming to identify crosslinking conditions that ensure both effective dissolution and improved stability. Methods: CPSE was prepared at 110 °C or 130 °C for 4, 8 or 12 h with uncrosslinked polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as the control. AG-CPSE-SDs and AG-PVA-SD were compared in terms of AG relative crystallinity (RC), surface free energy, hygroscopicity, dissolution and stability. Stability was evaluated after 30-day storage at 40 ± 2 °C/75 ± 5% RH. Results: Compared with AG-PVA-SD, AG-CPSE-SDs showed higher RC but lower surface free energy and hygroscopicity. SDs with lower crosslinking degrees had dissolution profiles similar to AG-PVA-SD, whereas those with higher crosslinking degrees showed significantly reduced dissolution rates. After storage, the dense network in highly crosslinked SDs hindered water entry and diffusion and restricted AG migration and recrystallization, thereby conferring better hygroscopic stability, interaction stability, recrystallization stability and dissolution stability. Notably, the SD using CPSE crosslinked at 130 °C for 4 h as the carrier balanced effective dissolution and enhanced stability. Conclusions: By tuning the crosslinking degree, SD stability can be improved without sacrificing drug dissolution. Moderate rather than maximal crosslinking achieves the optimal balance, providing a practical strategy for designing crosslinked carriers for SDs.

articles.title: Crisaborole-Loaded Nanoemulsion for Atopic Dermatitis: Localized Dermal Delivery of a Phosphodiesterase-4 Inhibitor.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Crisaborole (CRB) is a phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor used for the topical treatment of mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis (AD). However, its low aqueous solubility presents challenges for topical formulation and localized drug delivery. This study aimed to develop a CRB-loaded nanoemulsion (CRB-NE) and evaluate its physicochemical and biopharmaceutical characteristics, tolerability, and anti-inflammatory activity. Methods: CRB-NE (0.5% w/w) was developed using pseudo-ternary phase diagrams. Droplet size, morphology, rheological behavior, spreadability, and stability were characterized. Drug release and ex vivo permeation in human skin were evaluated. Biological compatibility was investigated using HaCaT keratinocytes and the hen's egg test-chorioallantoic membrane (HET-CAM) assay, while skin barrier compatibility was assessed in healthy volunteers. Anti-inflammatory activity was evaluated through IL-8 secretion in stimulated HaCaT cells and a xylene-induced ear inflammation model in mice. Results: CRB-NE showed a droplet size of 105.3 ± 6.7 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.287 ± 0.012, Newtonian flow behavior, and physical stability over 60 days. Approximately 80% of CRB was released following first-order kinetics. After 24 h, ex vivo experiments showed cutaneous retention of 1098.43 μg CRB/g skin/cm2 and cumulative permeation of 23.75 ± 4.44 μg/cm2. Keratinocyte viability exceeded 80% at CRB concentrations of 2.5-10 μg/mL, and HET-CAM results indicated low irritation potential. The vehicle did not adversely affect skin barrier measurements in healthy volunteers. CRB-NE significantly reduced IL-8 secretion in TNF-α-stimulated keratinocytes and attenuated erythema, inflammatory cell infiltration, edema, vascular congestion, and tissue damage in vivo. Conclusions: CRB-NE demonstrated favorable physicochemical properties, substantial cutaneous drug retention, and anti-inflammatory activity, supporting its potential as a localized topical delivery system.

articles.title: Functional Pharmacological Validation of Betahistine Release from Chitosan Microspheres Using an Isolated Guinea-Pig Gastric Smooth-Muscle Model.
articles.abstract: Background: Betahistine-loaded chitosan microspheres have previously demonstrated formulation-dependent drug release; however, conventional in vitro release testing does not establish whether the drug incorporated into the delivery system retains pharmacological activity. Methods: This study evaluated the time-dependent functional activity of four previously characterized betahistine-loaded chitosan formulations using isolated guinea-pig gastric smooth muscle strips. Microsphere quantities corresponding to an equivalent nominal amount of 10 mg betahistine were compared with free betahistine. Spontaneous contractile activity was continuously recorded and mean peak contractile force (Favr) and the area under the Favr-time curve were evaluated. Results: Free betahistine produced a pronounced early response followed by progressive attenuation. In contrast, all microsphere formulations produced gradually increasing and sustained responses, with higher observed Favr values than free betahistine at later observation times. Time-matched analysis revealed positive formulation-dependent associations between cumulative betahistine release and Favr (R2 = 0.8384-0.9914), whereas functional performance did not follow the rank order of drug loading. Conclusions: These findings provide functional evidence consistent with sustained availability of pharmacologically active betahistine from the chitosan microsphere formulations and support ex vivo functional assessment as a complementary approach to conventional in vitro release characterization.

articles.title: Oseltamivir-Based Organic Salts and Ionic Liquids: Physicochemical Properties, Cytotoxicity, and Neuraminidase Inhibition.
articles.abstract: Background: Neuraminidase (NA) inhibitors are widely used for the treatment of influenza, but the emergence of resistance and limitations in drug formulation can compromise their therapeutic performance. This study investigated whether counterion exchange can modulate the physicochemical properties, cytotoxicity, and NA-inhibitory activity of oseltamivir (OS) while preserving its covalent structure. Methods: Five OS-based ionic formulations, [OS][C1SO3], [OS][C3SO3], [OS][C6SO3], [OS][TolSO3], and [OS][CSA], were synthesized and characterized by NMR and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, with isolated yields ranging from 84 to 88%. Spectroscopic data confirmed the formation of the desired 1:1 salts and showed that the OS ethyl ester remained chemically intact. The formulations were evaluated for aqueous solubility, octanol/water partitioning, cytotoxicity toward MDCK-SIAT1 cells, and NA-inhibitory activity using a MUNANA-based assay against NAs from A(H1N1)pdm09, its H275Y oseltamivir-resistant variant, A(H3N2), and type B influenza viruses. Results: All formulations exhibited low cytotoxicity, with CC50 values above 1200 µM. All OS ionic formulations showed lower IC50 values than oseltamivir phosphate against all four influenza viruses, with improvements ranging from approximately 2.5- to 393-fold. [OS][TolSO3] showed the highest potency, reducing the IC50 by approximately 336-fold against H275Y virus NA and 393-fold against influenza B virus NA. IC90 values showed the same overall potency ranking, although improvements at 50% inhibition were not always proportionally maintained at 90% inhibition. Conclusions: Overall, counterion selection substantially influenced both the physicochemical and biological profiles of OS. [OS][TolSO3] provided the highest NA-inhibitory potency, whereas [OS][CSA] exhibited the most balanced overall profile, supporting counterion engineering as a potential approach to optimize oseltamivir-based ionic formulations.

articles.title: Stage-Specific Stability of Spray-Freeze-Dried Ovalbumin-Loaded Liposomes: Dissecting the Impact of Atomization, Freezing, and Drying on Cryoprotectant Performance.
articles.abstract: Objectives: Aqueous liposomal suspensions suffer from inherent physical and chemical instability, motivating the development of solid powder formulations. Spray-freeze-drying is a promising solidification technique; however, systematic investigations that isolate the impact of individual unit operations-atomization, freezing, and drying-on liposomal stability remain scarce. This study aimed to elucidate the stage-specific effects of each unit operation on the critical quality attributes of liposomal powders. Methods: Ovalbumin-loaded liposomes (O@L) prepared from DSPC, HSPC, or DPPC were processed using a self-developed microfluidic jet spray freezing tower coupled to a freeze dryer, with trehalose or mannitol as cryoprotectants. The effects of phospholipid composition, freezing temperature (-30 °C, -50 °C, and -70 °C), and freeze-drying cycle were assessed through the z-average, zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency (EE) of the reconstituted liposomes, as well as the morphology, crystallinity, residual moisture, and hygroscopicity of the resulting powders. Results: Atomization induced protein leakage from the trehalose formulations, whereas mannitol better preserved EE. During freezing, trehalose provided superior cryoprotection, as mannitol partially crystallized and failed to uniformly coat the vesicles. After drying, however, vesicles frozen at -70 °C exhibited fusion attributable to non-uniform cryoprotectant distribution; a moderate freezing temperature (-50 °C) combined with a stepwise primary drying program proved optimal. Trehalose-based powders displayed higher residual moisture and irreversible crystallization above ~60% RH, whereas crystalline mannitol ensured low, reversible hygroscopicity. Conclusions: The optimal condition for a single unit operation does not guarantee the best overall outcome; rational spray-freeze-drying process design requires balancing stage-specific effects.

articles.title: Enhanced Oral Bioavailability and Pharmacokinetics of Altrenogest via a Self-Nanoemulsifying Drug Delivery System.
articles.abstract: Background: Altrenogest (ALT) is a synthetic progestogen used to synchronize the oestrus of swine and horses. It is poorly absorbed orally and this severely limits its use. Self-nanoemulsifying drug delivery systems (SNEDDSs) have been identified as a potentially efficacious solution to these challenges, as they spontaneously generate fine oil-in-water nanoemulsions upon exposure to gastrointestinal fluids, thereby augmenting the dissolution and bioavailability of lipophilic drugs. Objective: In order to enhance the oral bioavailability of ALT, this study developed an ALT-loaded SNEDDS. The mechanisms of cellular uptake were investigated using MDCK monolayers, while in vivo pharmacokinetics and in situ intestinal perfusion studies in rats were conducted to assess systemic absorption, lymphatic transport potential, and intestinal permeation. Methods & Results: In vitro, ALT-SNEDDS demonstrated no significant toxicity towards MDCK cells at concentrations up to 12.8 μg/mL. The uptake of ALT-SNEDDS was found to be time- and energy-dependent, involving clathrin- and caveolae-mediated endocytosis. In rats, ALT-SNEDDS and its hydrated form, in comparison with an oil-based formulation, resulted in a significant elevation of Cmax and AUC, yielding 1.96- and 4.97-fold improvements in oral bioavailability. Lymphatic involvement was supported by a significant decrease in plasma concentration following cycloheximide blockade. Intestinal perfusion showed significantly higher Ka and Peff values for ALT-SNEDDS than free ALT, confirming enhanced small intestinal absorption. In an acute oral toxicity study, a single 40 mg/kg oral dose caused no apparent histopathological abnormalities in the major organs of rats. Conclusion: Collectively, the SNEDDS platform markedly facilitates ALT absorption and exhibits lymphatic transport propensity, providing a foundation for subsequent formulation optimization and for evaluation in the target species.

articles.title: Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Venetoclax in Pediatric Acute Myeloid Leukemia: Food Effects, Age-Related Pharmacokinetics, and Voriconazole-Mediated Drug-Drug Interactions.
articles.abstract: Background: Venetoclax (VEN), a selective B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, has been increasingly used off-label in pediatric patients with hematologic malignancies. However, its pharmacokinetic characteristics in pediatric patients remain insufficiently characterized. Methods: An adult VEN physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed and extrapolated to children using age-dependent physiological and CYP3A4 ontogeny data. The pediatric model was calibrated and evaluated using data from 76 children with AML (203 plasma concentrations) and subsequently applied to assess food effects, age-related pharmacokinetic differences, and VEN dose-reduction scenarios during VCZ co-administration. The clinical study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR1900027146 and ChiCTR2400080307). Results: The adult and pediatric models adequately reproduced the observed VEN concentration-time profiles. At 200 mg/m2, a normal-fat meal increased predicted AUCinf and Cmax by 2.74- and 1.77-fold, respectively, versus a low-fat meal. Children aged 2-<6 years had the highest exposure; AUCinf was 1.44- and 1.91-fold higher than in the 6-<12- and 12-<18-year groups, respectively. During VCZ co-administration, reducing VEN to 50% and 25% of the full dose decreased AUC0-168h by 36.8% and 60.5% and Cmax by 42.5% and 70.5%, respectively, with minimal changes in Tmax. Conclusions: The pediatric VEN PBPK model quantitatively characterized the effects of meal conditions, developmental age, and VCZ-mediated CYP3A inhibition on VEN pharmacokinetics. These findings support administration with a normal diet, closer safety monitoring in children aged 2-<6 years receiving 200 mg/m2, and model-informed evaluation of VEN dose reduction during concomitant VCZ therapy.

articles.title: Kinetic Model for Describing the Spring Effect and Incomplete Dissolution in Low-Solubility Drug Formulations Based on the Quality-by-Design (QbD) Approach.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Enhancing the bioavailability of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) with low solubility -classified under the Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) as class II and class IV -is a major challenge in pharmaceuticals development. Stabilizing APIs in amorphous form significantly increases their apparent solubility but results in complex dissolution profiles characterized by the "spring effect," a temporal high concentration peak during dissolution. These dissolution profiles are very challenging to be quantitatively evaluated due to the lack of appropriate mathematical models compatible with a Quality-by-Design (QbD) approach. Methods: A kinetic model was developed by considering the mechanistic aspects of the process. The model postulates three stages of the dissolution: hydration and dissolution of the amorphous API within the carrier, diffusion of the dissolved API into the medium, and equilibrium-driven interactions between the dissolved API and its thermodynamically stable crystalline form. Results: This model provides insights into release acceleration, slow final dissolution, and the spring effect, and elucidates scenarios where complete dissolution cannot be achieved due to the absence of sink conditions. While microscopic molecular phenomena -such as liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and polymeric crystallization inhibition -are extensively documented in the academic literature, their individual isolated parameters are inherently unobservable under routine pharmaceutical industrial and GMP testing conditions. To bridge this gap, the developed model establishes a robust, apparent kinetic framework that fits macroscopically observable dissolution profiles. Conclusions: This method provides a robust framework for interpreting drug release profiles and optimizing formulation development using a QbD approach, specifically supporting regulatory requirements and batch-to-batch consistency evaluations across similar polymer-matrix systems. The model enables the determination of kinetic parameters such as tmax and cmax, and explains their dependence on the actual pharmaceutical formulation.

articles.title: An Electrospun Core-Sheath/Janus-Integrated Hierarchical Structure for Asynchronous Mucosal Drug Delivery.
articles.abstract: Background: It is highly desirable to address the dual therapeutic needs of quickly alleviating clinical symptoms and providing long-lasting effects for motion sickness, as well as to overcome limitations of traditional electrospinning methods-such as easy drug mixing, poor zoning accuracy, and inadequate controlled-release capabilities. Methods: This study developed a self-developed trifluid electrospinning device. This device was used to create a dual-drug loaded nanofiber membrane containing diphenhydramine (DP) and scopolamine hydrobromide (SH), featuring a zoned structure composed of a polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) crescent side chamber, a round polylactic acid (PLA) sheath chamber, and a round PLA core chamber. Results: The results demonstrated that the fibers maintained an intact structure with distinct interfaces, allowing precise zoned loading of the two drugs, which were present in an amorphous dispersed state, indicating good compatibility and structural stability. The nanofiber membrane showed moderate mechanical strength and excellent hydrophilicity, making it suitable for oral mucosal drug delivery. Asynchronous drug delivery, featuring a rapid release of DP (53% at 1 h) and a sustained release of SH (85% at 12 h with no noticeable burst phenomenon), was demonstrated using two types of hierarchically structured nanofibers, each loaded with a single drug to facilitate measurement. The release mechanisms were disclosed for DP and SH from the tri-chamber hierarchical nanofibers. Cell studies confirmed its good biocompatibility. Conclusions: This work offers new insights and experimental evidence for developing an effective synergistic oral delivery system for motion sickness and advancing multifunctional nanocarrier drug delivery platforms.

articles.title: Osimertinib Optimal Dosing Through Population Pharmacokinetics in Virtual Patients with NSCLC: An Approach Integrating Multiple Studies.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Osimertinib is a third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) T790M mutations in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). A comprehensive population pharmacokinetic (popPK) model may inform dosing across patient populations. The objective was to develop an integrated popPK model for osimertinib in virtual patients with NSCLC and to evaluate the influence of patient characteristics on PK variability. Methods: Data were extracted from four published popPK studies of osimertinib in patients with NSCLC. A virtual cohort of 1000 patients from each study was simulated using the corresponding final popPK model, with covariate distributions reconstructed from the reported demographics, resulting in a total virtual cohort of 4000 patients. The primary outcome was the development of a popPK model using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling. Demographic and clinical covariates were evaluated for effects on PK variability. Results: A parent-metabolite one-compartment model best described osimertinib popPK. Body weight and serum albumin were significant covariates, with lower body weight and lower albumin concentrations associated with increased osimertinib plasma exposure. However, simulations demonstrated that the standard 80 mg once-daily dose maintained plasma concentrations within the literature-informed reference interval across all body weight and albumin subgroups. Conclusions: This popPK model suggests that despite significant effects of body weight and albumin on osimertinib exposure, routine dose adjustment may not be required. The standard 80 mg once-daily regimen maintains concentrations within the reference interval across diverse virtual patient populations with NSCLC, supporting current dosing recommendations. These model-informed findings warrant prospective validation with real-world clinical data to confirm generalizability.

articles.title: Cytoprotective Evaluation of Juglans regia L. Septum Extract and Development of Extract-Based Gels and Films for Topical Application.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives:Juglans regia L. septa are a rich source of phenolic compounds with potential skin-related biological activity. This study evaluated the cytoprotective activity of a lyophilised J. regia septum extract and developed extract-containing polymeric gels suitable for topical application and semi-solid extrusion (SSE) 3D printing. Methods: The extract was characterised by high-performance liquid chromatography with photodiode array detection (HPLC-PDA) and evaluated in H2O2-exposed human fibroblasts. Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)-, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC)-, and hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC)-based gels were prepared, and the selected formulation was processed into films by solvent casting and SSE 3D printing. The films were evaluated for thickness, moisture content, mechanical properties, and probe-film adhesiveness. Results: Ellagic acid was the predominant quantified phenolic compound (36.453 µg/mL). The free extract protected fibroblasts against H2O2-induced oxidative damage, with the greatest preservation of viable cells at 75 and 100 µg/mL. Increasing extract loading increased total quantified phenolic content in the gels from 10.95 to 27.98 µg/mL. The selected formulation was successfully processed into multilayer films. 3D-printed films showed numerically lower burst strength and breaking force per unit width than solvent-cast films, although pairwise differences were not significant. Hydration increased probe-film adhesiveness, while film moisture content decreased during 3 months of storage. Conclusions: These findings support the feasibility of incorporating cytoprotective J. regia extract into printable polymeric gels for topical film development.

articles.title: Multi-Cycle Dosimetry of the Albumin-Binding Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen Ligand [177Lu]Ludotadipep in Metastatic Androgen Pathway Modulator-Resistant Prostate Cancer with Adjusted Red Marrow Modeling.
articles.abstract: Purpose: This dosimetry study aimed to evaluate the organ-absorbed doses and safety profile of multiple doses of [177Lu]Ludotadipep, a novel PSMA-targeted radiopharmaceutical with an albumin-binding motif, in patients with metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant (mAPMR) prostate cancer. Methods: Twenty patients received a total of 68 cycles of [177Lu]Ludotadipep (3.70 GBq/cycle, up to six cycles, 8-week intervals), and dosimetry analysis was done for 67 cycles. Organ-absorbed doses were estimated using planar and SPECT/CT imaging and blood-based methods. Red marrow dose was calculated using a red marrow-to-blood activity concentration ratio (RMBLR) derived from a hematocrit-adjusted model for large molecules and cross-checked by comparison with data derived from quantitative SPECT/CT images and blood samples. Results: The hematocrit-adjusted RMBLR of 0.28 was consistent with physiologic expectations for albumin-bound agents for marrow dosimetry. The highest absorbed dose coefficients in the first cycle were in the salivary glands and kidneys (1.22 ± 0.530 and 0.674 ± 0.330 Gy/GBq, respectively), while the red marrow dose (0.0533 ± 0.0115 Gy/GBq) was lower. Summing the cycle-specific mean absorbed dose coefficients and multiplying by 3.70 GBq per cycle yielded projected six-cycle absorbed doses of 18.1 Gy for kidneys, 15.3 Gy for salivary glands, and 1.28 Gy for red marrow, all of which were below the reference dose constraints. Salivary gland dose coefficients declined significantly over repeated cycles (p  <  0.001), possibly from radiation-induced tissue damage. Conclusion: [177Lu]Ludotadipep demonstrates a favorable dosimetric safety profile across multiple cycles, up to six cycles. Application of an appropriately adjusted RMBLR for albumin-binding behavior allowed for reproducible red marrow dose estimation.

articles.title: BH3 Profiling Identifies Apoptotic Priming by SREBP-1/-2 Inhibition and Synergistic Anti-Glioblastoma Activity When Combined with ABT-263 In Vitro.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Glioblastoma exhibits profound therapy resistance driven in part by complex pro-survival signaling. We hypothesized that targeting lipid metabolism via SREBP-1/2 inhibition (fatostatin) might alter the apoptotic phenotype and facilitate an apoptotic response driven by BH3 mimetics (ABT-263) in glioblastoma in vitro. Methods: Dynamic BH3 profiling was performed to detect apoptotic priming. The combined inhibition of SREBP-1/2 and Bcl-xL/Bcl-2 was evaluated across 2- and 3-dimensional culture models. The cell lines used included established cell lines as well as primary cultures and glioma stem-like cells. Extracellular flux analysis was used to assess metabolic effects. Changes in migration were evaluated through time-lapse analysis, scratch, and Transwell assays. Results: BH3 profiling showed that treatment with fatostatin increased Bcl-xL/Bcl-2 reliance, while ABT-263 increased Mcl-1 dependence. The combination showed potent synergy in inhibiting viability and spheroid growth, driven at least in part by enhanced caspase-dependent apoptosis. Mechanistically, fatostatin induced dose-dependent Mcl-1 downregulation, sensitizing cells to ABT-263. Dual treatment suppressed oxidative phosphorylation and impaired cell migration, while exhibiting low toxicity in non-pathological cells. Conclusions: This study indicates that combined inhibition of SREBP-1/2 and Bcl-xL/Bcl-2 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of glioblastoma. The efficacy of this dual approach potentially lies in the downregulation of Mcl-1 induced by fatostatin and suppression of oxidative phosphorylation. Further studies are warranted.

articles.title: Engineering Chitosan-Coated PLGA Nanoparticles for Sustained Bupivacaine Delivery: Physicochemical Performance and a Preliminary Fibroblast Cytocompatibility Assessment.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Bupivacaine hydrochloride (Bupi-HCl) is a widely used local anesthetic; however, rapid diffusion from the site of administration and concentration-dependent cytotoxicity may limit its local therapeutic efficacy. This study aimed to develop chitosan-coated poly(D, L-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) nanoparticles for sustained Bupi-HCl delivery and to evaluate their physicochemical properties, release behavior, long-term stability, and cytocompatibility with fibroblasts. Methods: Bupi-HCl-loaded chitosan-coated PLGA nanoparticles (Bupi-CS-PLGA NPs) were prepared using a modified double-emulsion solvent-evaporation method and characterized by TEM, DLS, FTIR, DSC, XRD, encapsulation efficiency (EE), drug loading (DL), in vitro release, release kinetic modeling, 12-month physicochemical stability, and a preliminary MTT-based fibroblast cytocompatibility assessment. Results: Bupi-CS-PLGA NPs exhibited a predominantly spherical morphology, a mean particle size of 175.13 ± 8.10 nm, a PDI of 0.195 ± 0.026, and a zeta potential of +24.86 ± 1.90 mV. EE and DL were 80.00 ± 2.14% and 2.60 ± 0.11%, respectively. FTIR findings were consistent with physical incorporation of Bupi-HCl within the PLGA/chitosan matrix without evidence of new chemical bond formation, while DSC demonstrated differences in the thermal profiles of the nanoparticle formulations and XRD showed that Bupi-HCl was not detectable as a separate crystalline phase. The nanoparticles provided sustained Bupi-HCl release over 72 h, reaching approximately 79-80% cumulative release compared with 97-98% for free Bupi-HCl. Among the evaluated kinetic models, Modified Langmuir and RRSBW yielded the highest coefficients of determination (R2 = 0.9958 and 0.9952, respectively), while RRSBW showed the lowest total residual value (19.5851). Physicochemical characteristics were maintained during 12 months of storage at refrigerated and room temperatures. Within one experimental run, empty CS-PLGA NPs showed no decrease in MTT-derived signal across the tested concentration range. Bupi-CS-PLGA NPs showed lower MTT-derived signal at 250 and 500 µg/mL than at the two lower particle concentrations (62.5 and 125 µg/mL); particle-related assay interference was not excluded. Because free and encapsulated Bupi-HCl were not evaluated at dose-equivalent concentrations, their cytotoxic potency could not be directly compared, and these single-experiment findings are reported as a preliminary assessment. Conclusions: Bupi-CS-PLGA NPs provided sustained drug release and long-term physicochemical stability, together with a preliminary, assay-limited fibroblast MTT assessment. These findings support further evaluation of this biodegradable nanoparticle system for sustained local delivery of Bupi-HCl.

articles.title: 177Lu-Labeled HEDP-Functionalized Manganese-Substituted Maghemite Nanocarriers for Localized Radionuclide Therapy.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Effective intratumoral radionuclide therapy requires nanocarriers that enable stable radionuclide coordination and prolonged tumor retention. Integrating these properties with efficient magnetic heating within a single nanoplatform remains challenging because optimization of one property may compromise another. This study investigated whether manganese substitution could improve the magnetic heating performance of 1-hydroxyethylidene-1,1-diphosphonic acid (HEDP)-functionalized maghemite nanoparticles while preserving their suitability for radiopharmaceutical applications. Methods: Three MnxFe2-xO3 compositions (x = 0, 0.221, and 0.480) were evaluated in terms of their structural and physicochemical properties, colloidal stability, and magnetic heating performance. The most promising Mn-substituted formulation and the unsubstituted reference were evaluated by 177Lu radiolabeling, in vitro radiochemical stability testing, whole-body imaging, ex vivo biodistribution analysis, and therapeutic efficacy assessment in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice. Results: Moderate Mn substitution (x = 0.221) provided the most favorable combination of magnetic heating performance (SAR = 360 W g-1; ILP = 5.65 nH m2 kg-1) and colloidal stability. HEDP functionalization enabled direct radiolabeling with 177Lu, with labeling yields of 86-92% and radiochemical stability exceeding 94% after 96 h in saline and human serum. Following intratumoral administration, qualitative whole-body imaging showed persistent tumor-associated radioactivity for both nanoparticle formulations on days 5 and 14. On day 14, tumor-associated activity was 91.68 ± 0.73%ID and 84.53 ± 2.26%ID for [177Lu]Lu-NP1 and [177Lu]Lu-NP2, respectively, compared with 17.49 ± 8.06%ID for free [177Lu]LuCl3. Both nanoparticle formulations inhibited tumor growth compared with saline, with a more pronounced response and partial tumor regression in animals bearing smaller tumors at treatment initiation. Conclusions: Moderate Mn substitution improved magnetic heating performance and colloidal stability while preserving the radiochemical stability, intratumoral retention, and therapeutic efficacy of the 177Lu-labeled HEDP-functionalized nanocarriers. This nanoplatform warrants further investigation for intratumoral 177Lu therapy and its potential integration with magnetic hyperthermia.

articles.title: JAG1-siRNA-Lipid Nanoparticles Suppress Infantile Hemangioma Angiogenesis.
articles.abstract: Background: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most common benign vascular tumor of infancy, and propranolol, the current first-line treatment, requires prolonged twice-daily dosing and has adverse systemic effects. Methods: Using the public GSE127487 transcriptomic dataset together with weighted gene coexpression network analysis and protein-protein interaction network analysis, we identified JAG1, a principal endothelial Notch ligand, as the most connected node in the disease protein-protein interaction network, with elevated expression across all clinical stages of IH. To test its use as a drug target, we engineered a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) composed of SM-102/DSPC/cholesterol/DMG-PEG2000 that carried JAG1-specific siRNA. Results: At an N/P ratio of 8, the formulation efficiently encapsulated the siRNA, protected it from serum nucleases, and remained colloidally stable. LNP-mediated JAG1 knockdown reduced Matrigel network formation by hemangioma stem cells in vitro. In a hemangioma xenograft model, the intratumoral delivery of JAG1 siRNA reduced tumor volume by approximately 75%, tumor weight by approximately 80%, and microvessel density by more than half, without overt toxicity to the measures collected (body weight and clinical observation). Conclusions: In this preclinical model, JAG1 emerges as a credible therapeutic target, and LNP-delivered JAG1 siRNA is a promising gene-silencing strategy against IH angiogenesis.

articles.title: Early CYNC-1 Administration Attenuates Radiation-Induced Lung Inflammation and Subsequent Fibrotic Remodeling.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) involves inflammatory responses followed by fibrotic remodeling. We evaluated CYNC-1, a synthetic compound designed as a lipoxin A4 (LXA4) mimetic, for chemical stability, cellular activity, and attenuation of lung injury after irradiation. Methods: HeLa-derived L132 epithelial-like cells and THP1-Lucia NF-κB reporter monocytes were used for cell-based assays. Male C57BL/6 mice received a single 75-Gy focal lung irradiation. CYNC-1 administration began immediately after irradiation and continued every other day for 2 or 6 weeks. Lung injury was assessed using bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cellularity, micro-computed tomography, histopathology, and lung mechanics. Prednisolone and nintedanib served as reference treatments in the 2- and 6-week cohorts, respectively. Results: CYNC-1 maintained high HPLC area purity during light-protected ethanol storage for 48 h at -78, -20, and 4 °C. It increased survival of irradiated L132 cells and reduced LPS-induced NF-κB reporter activity. In L132 cells, treatment was associated with reduced NF-κB/MAPK and Smad2 phosphorylation and lower profibrotic marker expression. In mice, CYNC-1 reduced inflammatory cell accumulation and collagen deposition and improved lung structure and mechanics. Conclusions: Early and continued CYNC-1 administration attenuated lung inflammation and subsequent fibrotic remodeling in this focal irradiation model. The signaling findings are associative, and FPR2 dependence and efficacy against established fibrosis remain to be established. Validation in primary human lung cells, clinically relevant fractionated irradiation models, animals of both sexes, and tumor models is needed to determine suitability as a normal-tissue protectant, including preservation of antitumor efficacy.

articles.title: Drug-Induced CYP2D6 Phenoconversion Among Individuals with a Psychiatric Disorder: Prevalence and Association with Psychological Distress.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Phenoconversion extends pharmacogenomics beyond genetic variation by accounting for non-genetic factors that can also dynamically alter metabolism, influence treatment response, adverse effect risk and overall patient outcomes. CYP2D6 phenoconversion is problematic in people with psychiatric conditions due to the high comorbidity and polypharmacy burden in this population and the significant proportion of psychiatric medications that inhibit CYP2D6 metabolism or are directly metabolised by CYP2D6. Our aim was to estimate the prevalence of CYP2D6 phenoconversion, the association with comorbidity and polypharmacy and the impact on mental health outcomes. Methods: Using UK Biobank data, phenoconversion was estimated by applying a standard multiplication factor to genotype-based activity scores according to CYP2D6 inhibitor use, and associations with comorbidity and polypharmacy were assessed. Findings were validated by meta-analysis (PROSPERO, CRD420251177663). Regression analyses assessed the relationship between CYP2D6 phenoconversion and psychological distress, measured using a modified version of the PHQ-4 from UK Biobank. Results: Seventeen percent (n = 5942) of UK Biobank participants with a self-reported psychiatric/psychological disorder (n = 35,338) were estimated to be subject to CYP2D6 phenoconversion. CYP2D6 phenoconverted individuals had higher comorbidity and polypharmacy medications, each p < 0.001. Twelve studies were included in our meta-analysis, producing a pooled prevalence of 17% (n = 7498, 95% CIs:12-24%, I2 = 98%) and 13% (n = 1633, 95% CIs: 11-15%, I2 = 24.2%) in a more homogeneous adult-only subgroup. CYP2D6 phenoconversion was significantly associated with higher modified PHQ-4 scores from UK Biobank (p < 0.001, r = 0.067), with individuals subject to phenoconversion scoring 10% higher (IRR 1.10, 95% CIs: 1.07-1.13) and having 19% greater odds of higher psychological distress scores (modified PHQ-4 score ≥ 6) (OR 1.19, 95% CIs: 1.11-1.28). Conclusions: Overall, CYP2D6 inhibitor use is common in psychiatry, and our findings support the need to consider phenoconversion.

articles.title: Co-Occurrence Patterns of Symptom and Functional Burden Associated with Tofacitinib and Upadacitinib: A Multidimensional Analysis of Spontaneous Reports in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pharmacovigilance studies typically evaluate adverse events as isolated drug-event pairs, potentially overlooking symptoms and functional impairments reported concurrently within the same case. We investigated co-reported adverse event patterns for tofacitinib and upadacitinib in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Methods: FAERS reports submitted between 2004 and 2025 were included if tofacitinib or upadacitinib was recorded as the primary suspect drug for RA. Disproportionality analysis was integrated with three co-occurrence network approaches, Bayesian network analysis, and time-to-onset (TTO) analysis. Methotrexate served as an indication-matched comparator. Network analyses were stratified by reporter and submission type, and TTO was reassessed for the common 2019-2025 period. FAERS signals were also compared descriptively with Canada Vigilance data. Results: We identified 57,438 tofacitinib-related and 29,869 upadacitinib-related reports, yielding 316 and 413 positive Preferred Term signals, respectively. In the tofacitinib networks, fatigue was consistently associated with pain, mood-related terms, treatment experience, and gastrointestinal and infectious events. Upadacitinib reports exhibited a distinct pattern, with falls, pain, functional limitations, and injuries occupying central positions. Reduced grip strength, decreased joint range of motion, and loss of personal independence formed a recurrent functional cluster. Methotrexate networks were primarily organized around disease-activity terms. The median reported TTO was 34 days for tofacitinib and 115 days for upadacitinib; corresponding values for the 2019-2025 period were 59 and 115 days, respectively. These intervals should not be interpreted as true onset latency or as established hazard patterns. Conclusions: Co-reporting analysis yielded insights beyond individual disproportionality signals. Tofacitinib reports were predominantly characterized by fatigue and associated symptoms, whereas upadacitinib reports more prominently featured functional limitations, falls, and injuries.

articles.title: Gelled Oil-in-Water Microemulsions Stabilized with Natural Surfactant Decyl Glucoside as Cutaneous Nanocarriers for Cinnamon Bark Essential Oil: Formulation and Comprehensive Pharmacotechnical Characterization.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cinnamon bark essential oil (CEO) possesses antimicrobial, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties. However, its topical application is limited by poor aqueous solubility, volatility, and chemical instability. The aim of this study was to develop gelled oil-in-water microemulsions stabilized with Decyl Glucoside for the cutaneous delivery of CEO and to evaluate their physicochemical and pharmaceutical characteristics. Methods: Pseudoternary phase diagrams were constructed to identify the microemulsion regions using Decyl Glucoside, propylene glycol, CEO, isopropyl myristate, and water. Selected CEO-loaded microemulsions were characterized in terms of droplet size, polydispersity index, zeta potential, refractive index, viscosity, and apparent pH, and were subsequently gelled with Aerosil® 200. The resulting gelled microemulsions were evaluated for CEO content, apparent pH, rheological and textural properties, spreadability, in vitro release and skin permeation studies. The short-term stability of both liquid and gelled microemulsions was also assessed over 45 days. Results: Three CEO-loaded oil-in-water microemulsions were selected from the isotropic regions of the pseudoternary phase diagrams and successfully transformed into homogeneous gelled systems without phase separation. CEO incorporation increased the storage modulus and yield stress of the gelled formulations compared with the corresponding blank systems. The surfactant-to-cosurfactant ratio markedly influenced the rheological properties, mechanical strength, and in vitro release and skin permeation of CEO. Among the investigated formulations, MEG-CEO-2 provided the best balance between mechanical properties, CEO release, and skin permeation. Both liquid and gelled microemulsions maintained their principal physicochemical characteristics during the 45-day stability assessment. Conclusions: Decyl Glucoside-stabilized gelled microemulsions exhibited physicochemical and pharmaceutical properties supporting their further investigation as topical delivery systems for CEO. The results demonstrate that the surfactant-to-cosurfactant ratio can be used to tailor formulation performance, supporting a rational approach for the development of CEO-loaded dermal delivery systems. However, preservation of the biological activities of CEO following incorporation into these systems remains to be experimentally established.

articles.title: Multifunctional Hyaluronic Acid-Modified Pterostilbene Nanoliposomes for Enhanced Dermal Delivery and Extracellular Matrix Protection.
articles.abstract: Background: Skin aging involves extracellular matrix (ECM) deterioration, including collagen loss and disrupted glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan homeostasis. Pterostilbene (PTE) has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, but its topical use is limited by poor aqueous solubility and limited skin delivery. We developed hyaluronic acid (HA)-modified, PTE-loaded nanoliposomes (HA-LP-PTE) and evaluated their association with dermal fibroblasts, retention in skin, and effects on ECM-related responses. Methods: HA-LP-PTE was prepared by high-pressure microfluidization and assessed for size, morphology, zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency. Fluorescence microscopy was used to examine fibroblast-associated fluorescence of FITC-labeled HA-LP-PTE and non-HA-modified PTE-loaded liposomes (LP-PTE). Skin retention was assessed using Franz diffusion cells. ECM-related changes were analyzed in UV-irradiated ex vivo skin and fibroblasts using staining techniques and RT-qPCR. Results: HA-LP-PTE had a mean diameter of 55.44 ± 0.81 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.120 ± 0.009, and an encapsulation efficiency of 99.34 ± 0.51%. At 4 h, fibroblast-associated fluorescence was higher than with LP-PTE (p = 0.040) and was reduced by free HA or incubation at 4 °C. After 12 h, dermal PTE retention was 4.08-fold higher than free PTE and 1.74-fold higher than LP-PTE. HA-LP-PTE increased all six ECM components examined. Chondroitin sulfate and perlecan met the Q criterion for synergy, and several ECM synthesis-related genes were upregulated. Conclusions: HA modification improved PTE delivery beyond liposomal encapsulation alone, with greater fibroblast-associated fluorescence and higher PTE retention in viable skin than LP-PTE. ECM and gene-expression findings also indicated matrix-related activity. HA-LP-PTE may enhance topical PTE delivery and attenuate UV-induced ECM loss.

articles.title: Molecular Interactions of Bioactive Peptides with Proteins and DNA.
articles.abstract: Background: This study investigates the molecular recognition of two biologically active peptides (P1 and P2) by key biomacromolecular targets. The studied peptides were previously identified in Babylon snail hydrolysates and have been shown to exhibit antioxidant and cytotoxic activities against Caco-2 colorectal cancer cells. Given their reported biological potential, we decided to investigate both compounds from a different perspective. Their interactions with human serum albumin (HSA), alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AAG), lysozyme (LYS), immunoglobulin G (IgG), and DNA were evaluated. Methods, Results and Conclusions: Spectroscopic analyses revealed concentration-dependent binding of the studied peptides to plasma proteins under investigations. Notably, peptide binding did not substantially alter the secondary structure of the target proteins, indicating that complex formation occurs without significant structural perturbation. Molecular docking further supported the formation of peptide-protein complexes, highlighting the contribution of hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic contacts to molecular recognition. The combined spectroscopic and docking results were consistent with a predominantly non-intercalative, possibly minor-groove-associated interaction with ctDNA. Taken together, these findings provide a comparative physicochemical characterization of the interactions of P1 and P2 with selected proteins and ctDNA. These findings provide insight into the molecular recognition properties of P1 and P2 and support further investigation of their biological relevance.

articles.title: Nitrogen-Drag-Assisted Crosslinking by Glucose to Obtain Bovine Serum Albumin-SGI-1027 Nanoparticles.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Nanoparticle (NP) technology is a promising tool against atherosclerosis, an inflammatory disease of large- and medium-sized arteries and an underlying cause of cardiovascular disease. Notably, DNA methyltransferase inhibitors such as SGI-1027 are anti-inflammatory. SGI-1027 tissue target specificity and potency may improve when loaded into an NP. We have previously shown that SGI-1027 nanoencapsulation with serum albumin NPs is anti-inflammatory in cell culture and anti-atherogenic in vivo. Nonetheless, nanoencapsulation relied on glutaraldehyde, which limits pharmacological applications. To increase NP biocompatibility, we assessed an alternative crosslinking method based on glucose and solvent drag to synthesize bovine serum albumin (BSA) NP loaded with SGI-1027. We assessed the physicochemical and functional parameters of BSA NPs loaded with increasing SGI-1027 doses (0, 0.05, and 0.1 mg).
